speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
That commencing on Wednesday, June 1, and on every sitting day thereafter until the end of this session, the hours of sitting shall be as follows:
Monday: 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.; 2.30 to 6 p.m.; and 3 to 10 p.m.
Tuesday: 11 a.m. to 1 pun.; 2.30 to 6 p.m. and 8 to 10 p.m.
Wednesday: 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.; and 2.30 to 6 p.m.
Thursday: 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.; 2.30 to 6 p.m. and 8 to 10 p.m.
Friday: 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.; and 2.30 to 6 p.m. and that the provisions of standing order 2 (1) and 6 (3) be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a reference to the motion. With the leave of the house I would ask that my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs move to amend the motion in its present form deleting the words "and 6 (3)" from the second last line. The application will be made later on unless it is now accepted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: The motion will be taken as moved with the deletion of the words "and 6 (3)".

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to do more at this time than introduce the motion and make one or two very short observations. I will endeavour to cover the matters that may be raised during the course of the debate on the motion when I have the opportunity to reply at the conclusion of the debate.
I would point out that last year a motion like this was introduced on the 92nd day of the session. Today is the 91st day of this session. While the uncompleted portion of the legislative program and the various items remaining to be dealt with by the house was, I think, somewhat longer last year than this, I might point out that last year prorogation took place on July 18.
I express the hope that we shall be able so to order the progress of the debate on the
various items referred to in the speech from the throne that we shall be able to cover them with expedition without in any way sacrificing the fullest debate. By that I do not mean in any way to direct or to hamper the fullest debate. I anticipate that by about the first week of July we should be able to conclude the business of this session.
There are some who speak of delaying actions which have taken place. I do not take any stand in that regard. I simply point out that when the progress of business in this house is compared with that in the mother of parliaments it is often forgotten that under their rules the time for debate on the speech from the throne, the budget and the like generally runs from two to three days; whereas under our rules the speech from the throne requires 12 days, including the opening day and the day devoted to the mover and the seconder. The budget debate requires eight days. Then we have private members' Mondays, of which we have had six. They are provided for under the rules. There are private members' Thursdays, of which we have had three.
Then we have a procedure which is not followed in the British house to the same extent, and certainly not to the degree provided for by our rules. We have six supply motions of two days each. Up to the present date we have had five of those supply motions. In other words, under the rules as they are, regardless of whether or not we agree that they should be as they are, so far this session we have had 39 days which have been taken up as a result of the rules which exist at the moment.
Then on supplementary estimates a longer time has been taken. Usually those estimates in general have been pretty well covered in the previous session. This year, however, 10 days have been devoted to supplementary estimates and three days to interim supply. On the other hand, the other measures that have been before the house have taken, generally speaking, one to two days with the exception of the resolution and bill on the Trans-Canada Highway Act, which took four days, and the resolution and bill on the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, which took eight days.
I am not making any criticism of the fact that the debate on that resolution and bill took eight days, but I do not think there would be many who would deny that at the

Business of the House
end of two days almost everything that could have been said had been said.
However, that is what parliament is for, and I am not raising any objection. When I said a few moments ago that I hoped we could so order arrangements for the rest of the session as to finish by the time I indicated, what I had in mind was that we adopt a kind of voluntary sacrifice of opportunity in not carrying on debates beyond that limit within which every possible argument has been advanced. However, even on the basis of the record to date I still believe it will be possible, with the co-operation of hon. members in all parts of the house, to bring about prorogation early in July.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house have listened with interest to the remarks made by the Prime Minister on the motion to have the house sit in the mornings and begin a drive to bring the session to an end. In that respect I should like to say that we will co-operate to the fullest extent to the end that the session may be brought to a conclusion early in July if that is possible or, if not, we will come back for a fall session if it is the wish of the house.
There are some things that must be kept in mind. In the first place, we feel very strongly that certain matters must be debated at greater length than others. The Prime Minister has brought to the attention of the house a number of matters that have taken some time, and having sat on the other side of the house as he does now I realize, of course, the position in which the government finds itself. I can well remember how former prime ministers have sometimes taken the exact position which the present Prime Minister is taking now, but with very little cooperation from the opposition in those days. At that time the opposition felt that certain items of legislation should be discussed at greater length.
There is one thing I wish to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister in this regard. While it is true that we have taken 91 days to discuss certain matters, including 39 days in the discussion of the matters he mentioned earlier, 10 days for supplementary estimates, 3 days for interim supply, 4 days, I believe he said, for the Trans-Canada Highway Act and 8 days for the discussion of university grants, I should like to draw to his attention the fact that in the discussion of a number of these pieces of legislation there were more speakers from the government side of the house than from the opposition and the C.C.F. put together. I have reference now to the debate on university grants, where

we were met not only speaker for speaker but in some instances by a proportion of two or three to one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
Oh, no; just
speaker for speaker.

speechtext:
I am not complaining at all about that situation, but I am saying to the Prime Minister that unquestionably there is no doubt that if there has been any delay in a number of these cases it is not our fault. I might also refer to the agricultural estimates, which we were almost ready to put through the other evening, but speaker after speaker on the other side of the house rose and held up those estimates.
There are one or two other things I should like to draw to the attention of the house. We do not have before us yet a complete list of the items of legislation that have to be dealt with, but if effect is to be given to the speech from the throne we do know there are a number of items of legislation and, of course, the vast majority of the estimates which must be disposed of. There is, of course, the bill of rights which will require some considerable discussion, and if it is the intention to proceed with that bill at this session I hope the government will see fit to send it to a committee of the house.
Then there is the very important revision of the Civil Service Act, which I am sure is of tremendous importance to all of us. I am wondering whether any consideration has been given by the government to the introduction of this bill, giving it first reading and referring it to a committee so it might be studied, as was done with other measures during the past two sessions. I think that is a matter which might well be considered.
There is, too, the matter of capital punishment which was to have been debated further, and upon which there was to have been a free vote by all members of parliament. Within the last two weeks no indication has been given of what action is to be taken in that respect, so that debate has been left hanging, if I might use an expression.
I cannot resist drawing to the attention of the Prime Minister three matters that are on the order paper today. First there is his own motion for these sittings, and on the opposite page there are two motions to set up committees, one concerning the committee on agriculture and colonization-

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: No, it has been set up.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
-or to refer to the committee on agriculture and colonization certain matters concerning the prices of farm

machinery. The other motion is tor the establishment of a select committee on broadcasting. It seems to me that at least the second matter, if not both matters, could have been brought forward a long time ago. We on this side of the house have been asking for the establishment of the broadcasting committee, and to establish it when we are going to sit in the morning and when, in some cases, it will be very difficult for the committee to sit while the house is sitting, seems to me to be placing great difficulty in the way of the work of this committee.
I know the Prime Minister is extremely anxious to give the committees of the house work so that his members, and all the members of the house, can be kept actively engaged. The setting up of this very important committee now gives some indication of the fact, in the first place, that it will not be possible, if we are to complete our work by the first week of July, to deal effectively with the important matters which should be referred to that committee. In so far as the price of farm machinery is concerned, I do not know why it was not possible to refer that matter to the committee earlier.
I could perhaps say there are some matters which, in our opinion, could be disposed of rather quickly and on which long debates would certainly not be necessary. I will not take the time of the house by mentioning them now. I have given some indication of them to the house leader. There are others, on the other hand, where lengthier debates will be necessary and a greater length of time will be taken up in the consideration of what we believe are important matters.
In the light of all this I want to conclude by saying that we will co-operate to the fullest extent. We feel that we should take the time which in our opinion is essential to dispose of some of the matters which are already on the order paper, and some other matters which although not on the order paper have been mentioned in the speech from the throne.
Perphaps I could make this request of the Prime Minister. In the light of what I have said and what others may say, might it not be advisable to give effect to this motion on Monday June 6 rather than on Wednesday, June 1? However, if the Prime Minister feels that it should remain as it is, we on this side of the house will support it.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this corner of the house have listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made by the Prime Minister and that by the spokesman for the official
Business of the House
opposition. It is quite obvious that, as far as the government is concerned-and now with the agreement of the official opposition- everything will be done to get rid of parliament as soon as possible.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, as is customary at a certain point in every session, we have the Prime Minister introducing a motion such as the one we have before us this afternoon, to the effect that starting on Wednesday and henceforth, Monday through Friday, the House of Commons shall meet at eleven o'clock in the morning.
I expected something different from the present Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. He has had a unique experience. Today he is the Prime Minister of Canada. It is not so long ago that for a short time he was leader of the opposition. For many years prior to that time he was a private member. He therefore knows perhaps better than anyone else in the House of Commons the responsibilities, the work and the strain involved in being a private member, leader of the opposition and Prime Minister. Yet with that knowledge and experience he introduces today this motion we have before us.
We in this group in this corner of the house want to say that the motion is absolutely unfair and unrealistic. It is designed to do something that I never thought the present Prime Minister would ever do, namely to bring about a situation in support of cabinet government and not of House of Commons government.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: Sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
That, Mr. Speaker, is the point to which I am coming. There are too many members in this House of Commons who want to go home instead of staying here to do the job for which they were elected. Not one of us was ever compelled to accept a nomination. We accepted that responsibility knowing that we live in a democracy and that, should we be elected, 265 men and women of Canada are given the power and authority by 17,500,000 people in Canada to endorse laws, rescind laws, amend laws, impose taxation and spend the taxpayers' money. When we accept nomination and are elected, there is no question in our minds as to whether we have to sit in Ottawa for two months, five months, eight months or a year. Then why is it that in the most responsible jobs, the greatest honour that a man or woman can have, we are expected to try to see how fast we can get out because we do not like the heat or the humidity of summer in parliament? Why is it that when there is such a fight by the trade unions for respectable hours

Business of the House of work, those who have the greatest responsibility in Canada-those who make the law, amend the law, impose taxation and spend the money-should be told every year, I think it is after 90 days, or 91 days, "You will have to speed up"?
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I want to say this to the Prime Minister. The right hon. gentleman knows that a private member of the House of Commons has responsibility to his constituents; he has to conduct correspondence; he has research work to carry on; he has speeches to prepare, and in addition he has committee work. At the present time- the same day this motion is being moved by the Prime Minister

there are 11 standing committees of the House of Commons which have not yet completed their work or submitted their final reports. These committees have to meet. In addition there is the special committee on defence expenditure. Notice has been given regarding the committee which is to consider the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We understand there is to be a committee on the bill of rights. We know the Minister of Justice intends that after second reading the important legislation on the Combines Investigation Act will go to the banking and commerce committee.
However, we are to meet at 11 a.m. When do the special committees or the standing committees meet? They meet from 9.30 until 11, or when the house is meeting.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: So what?

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
I want to say to some hon. members, because I know where that interruption came from, that if they got up and came here as early as I do they would not be rushed half as often as they are.
There are 11 committees which have not yet reported. There are two or three, perhaps four, special committees. If this house is to meet at eleven on Monday through Friday, then I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how does an ordinary member take care of his work on a constituency basis? How does he find time to attend to grievances, attend committees and attend the House of Commons at the same time? There is only one thing a member can do on that basis-

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: That is, shut up.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: That is exactly what they want us to do, shut up.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
Well, we have no intention of shutting up on any matter which we feel is of importance to this country and with which we were elected to deal. Whoever said that may have that acceptance of responsibility.


It is not the way responsibility is accepted in this group. We in this group want to do the job for which we were elected-

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: Why don't you try it?

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: -and that is to deal properly, intelligently-

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: Impossible.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
-with all bills, all expenditures, all taxation and all committees. Further, I am going to say this. A person who is a responsible member of the House of Commons-and I think the majority fall into this category-cannot take care of his correspondence, do his research, prepare for speeches which are to be delivered extemporaneously and not read, and attend committees from early in the morning until late at night.
I know there are those who would like to get back to their private business. That is their responsibility. When they stood for election to the House of Commons it meant spending whatever time was required in the House of Commons and, I say, it means working decent hours under decent conditions and not being forced, as parliament is every year at a certain time, to go home. I would like to go home, too.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
But I am not going as long as there is a job to do here for which I was elected and for which I am being paid. I would like through you, Mr. Speaker, to ask the Prime Minister whether he will not face up to what should have been faced a long time ago, and something which certainly will have to be faced in the very near future. Canada is a young country, a country with a growing population, growing potentialities and, I think, a growing influence. Incidentally, too, there are growing expenditures. Sometimes I am amazed when some of our members do not recognize that 265 people here are dealing, I believe, with a $6,500 million business. Not only that, but by the laws we make and the policies we follow we are dealing with the lives of 17,500,000 people. In a situation like this we cannot just say "I move that we start meeting earlier and sit longer". What is of importance on the last day of the session was just as important on the first day of the session and is entitled to the same thought, the same deliberate, conscientious, intelligent decision.
I imagine, Mr. Speaker, you have gathered that we are opposed to this motion. I ask the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister to recall his experience during his long years as a private member and the little while during which he was leader of the official opposition. Does he not agree the time

has come for a change in the sittings of this house? Does he not believe that the rights of the people of Canada are such that we should not hurry away from here because we want to get home for the summer to avoid the heat and humidity of Ottawa, which are pretty rough? Does he not think we have the responsibility of arranging the sittings of parliament to provide for the fullest consideration of the people's business?
There is a lot of work still before the House of Commons. I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on the work of the committees. They have improved and have more freedom than under the previous administration. Their reports are splendid. But there is still much work to be done. The estimates of only one department have been passed. We have passed only one department, agriculture, and are still on the first item of the estimates of the Post Office Department. The major legislation is still to be discussed. Instead of coming before the house, apparently by some agreement with the official opposition, to set a deadline by which to be out of here, and instead of considering our private interests, the temperature and engaging in collusion, we should consider the people's business.
If we cannot be out of here on a normal basis within a month or two let us use common sense and adjourn the house during the middle or end of this month and come back at the end of September or early in October or November. Is it not time that we as members of parliament thought of others? Do we ever think of the staff, the clerks, the stenographers, the security officers? Does the Prime Minister ever think of the press gallery? Oh, yes, I know he does.
For many years the hundreds of employees involved in the work of the House of Commons and Senate have not had a holiday with their children because parliament sits until the end of July or well into August. I do not care from what point of view you approach the question; the course of action I have referred to on the part of the government is unfair to the staff. We are the 265 men and women who make, change and break the laws, who impose taxation and spend the public money. We do not initiate it, but we have to vote on it. On that basis each of us should have a full opportunity to discharge his responsibilities to his constituents, to the committees of which he is a member and to this house.
Do you know what happens? Three or four times a week in the press mention is made of there being only 31, 32 or 33 members in the chamber. There may be a few laggards, but the majority of hon. members
Business of the House
do their work even if they are not present in the chamber to be counted. They work in committees, are involved in research and are taking care of grievances. Now the government wants to increase the burden. I say to the Prime Minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that he has betrayed the principle of parliamentary rule and is leading us now to more definite cabinet rule.
Every government likes to get rid of parliament. I ask that this motion be not accepted. I urge every hon. member to remember that when he ran for parliament he agreed to serve the people of Canada. That does not mean for four or six months but for whatever period is required to give proper consideration to the people's business. That is the view of this group. So strongly are we of this view that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier):
That the motion be amended by deleting, in line 2 thereof, the words "Wednesday, June 1" and substituting therefore the words "Friday, July 1".

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to endorse the amendment proposed by my colleague. I noticed that while he spoke a number of backbench supporters of the government hollered at him to shut up. I regret that there are a number of hon. gentlemen who are more loyal to their political party than they are to the interests of the Canadian people.
One reason for my supporting the amendment is that I feel it is unwise to even attempt to accomplish the aim the Prime Minister has outlined and wind up our business in the early part of July. I know there is much important legislation yet to consider, and I had hoped that even more legislation would be introduced this session.
We have already received notice of amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. This is of importance and will call for extended debate. We were informed in the speech from the throne that we are to be faced with a bill of rights, and even the Prime Minister is under no illusions in this regard. The debate on this legislation is going to be extended, and this is putting it mildly. We had also hoped that at this session of the house we would have many other items of legislation in line with the undertakings that were given to the electorate both in 1957 and in 1958.
Meetings are about to begin of the very important committee to deal with the procedure of the house. I hope the Prime Minister does not imagine that this is a light matter; that this is going to be easily dispensed with at the threat of the whip of the government. I can assure him that the opposition intends,

Business of the House
as the saying goes, to dig in its heels on the committee dealing with procedure, because this is very important in a democracy. I hope this important committee will have no intention of being dictated to, or of being informed that it will have to wind up and have the house accept its recommendations before July 8 or any other date.
The very important committee on atomic energy has yet to hold its initial meeting. We have the very important committee considering the defence policies of the government of the day, and we cannot be expected to conclude this in any way, shape or form by July 8. We have information that the Immigration Act is very much in need of radical revision and that our whole immigration policy needs a debate of considerable extent on the part of the House of Commons. We expect this, and I do not see how we can arrange it before July 8.
We have had assurances that the government is interested in the small businessman, and we are expecting legislation in this regard. We have had assurances that the government is vitally concerned with the problems of our municipal governments, and we expect legislation in this regard at this session. We do not want it in the election session of next winter; we want it now, and the Canadian people expect the legislation now. We intend to remain here until we get the legislation.
We have had information that the government has a great ear for the pleas of agriculture. We intend to remain here until we see some legislation in this regard. We have had assurances that the veterans will be adequately dealt with. We intend to remain here until the veterans receive a little more than they have received hitherto from this government. We have had assurance that this government is intending to do something with regard to the tight money situation. We intend to remain here until some action is forthcoming in this regard. We have had an investigation in the field of social security. The Clark report has been tabled. We expect legislation implementing some of the findings that were reviewed in the Clark report. We have the important matter of our deteriorating foreign trade balance. We expect legislation at this session in regard to federal aid to education. Then there is the assurance of the Prime Minister and other leading members of the government that there will be a new deal in relation to national highways. We have, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has already said, many committees meeting. I can attend only about half the ones I am on.
I have four youngsters at home. They are in their teens. I have been here since 1953,
[Mr. HegierJ
Mr. Speaker, and the family at home is getting sick and tired of remaining at home throughout the hot months of July and August and never knowing whether the father is coming home in order to live with his family at the only holiday time that a family has in Canada these days. Year after year we have to live in hope that some nice morning the Prime Minister will get out on the right side of the bed and will give us and our families a break. It is becoming intolerable. I know a number of men, Mr. Speaker, who were going to be candidates in the next national election, but who have now informed me that because of their domestic responsibilities they will no longer be available.
Are we to have only men without families representing the families of Canada in this House of Commons, or are we going to decide that the responsible thing is to plan and to have, as most other democracies have and as most other democratic parliaments have arranged for, certain months in which we meet, and organize our business accordingly?
The government of Germany meets for 10 months of the year and has eight weeks of recess. The members of the Bundestag know their working period ahead of time. The members at Westminster in Britain, the mother of parliaments, are advised; they know when they will be home and when they will have to meet their responsibilities of office. Yet we in the Canadian parliament are supposed to be forever liable and subject to the personal wish of one man, the Prime Minister. I know that when I speak now I have the support, if not the spoken support, of many of his supporters in the government who are willing and anxious for the Prime Minister to announce that the government has agreed that we ought to have a little bit of law and order as to when we meet and when we adjourn.
As has been mentioned, this is a $6 billion business. I feel that we have no right to go through form and procedure such as the speech from the throne, the budget debate and the supply motions and then wind up everything else of any consequence in as big a hurry as we can. I realize there are members of this house who belong to the legal profession, and there are a few of those- and only a small number of them-who are interested in the assizes in the fall. They do not like the house to meet at the same time the fall assizes are meeting. However, most of the members of the house who belong to the legal profession have not yet reached the point where they have any interest at all in the fall assizes. I feel that those members of the House of Commons who are

leading lawyers should not have had such undue influence on the government-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
-in bringing about the introduction of a motion of this kind. Over the coffee table and elsewhere we often meet with members who are supporters of the government, and we know that most of them agree with our contention that there should be some order and planning, and that the interests of this limited number of individuals should be disregarded. If a member of the house regards his law practice as so remunerative and important that he cannot attend to the business of the nation, I would recommend that he should not accept nomination at election time.
We have laws in the interests of our working people. I agree that many of them only get one week's vacation a year, though some get several weeks. A very limited number get three weeks' vacation a year. However, the members of the House of Commons receive no holidays that are determined by law. We often obtain what holidays we do get because of the particular wishes of the government, and more often than not these holidays are useless so far as our domestic responsibilities are concerned.
I am the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and I should like to refer to the wonderful example of a man who died a little over a year ago, the late Ernest E. Winch. He was elected to the legislature of British Columbia in 1933, I believe, and from the time he was first elected his only source of income was the allowance he received as a member of the legislative assembly of British Columbia. He devoted the whole of his life to the public interest, and I think he should be an example to all members of this house, because we are in receipt of a much greater income than he was in his day. I should like to think that members of the house would not be adverse to returning here on October 1 and remaining here for the months of October and November. Let us have the months of July, August and September off, as well as the month of December. If we decide that this is to be the policy we can organize our business and our affairs to accommodate the conditions of our work in the House of Commons.
I believe that at this time the house would be most unwarranted in adopting the recommendation of the Prime Minister. I plead with members of the house to be more interested in the business of the nation from the long term point of view and in the responsibility that faces each member of the house, and to disregard at least for this one
Business of the House
occasion the dictation of the government and vote in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not desire to detain the house for more than a few minutes, because I have noticed that when we have a motion on the order paper to save time or to prolong the time for discussion a substantial part of the time we would save or that would be gained is taken up in discussion of the way to save or prolong it. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will not be long; but the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East in one respect at least were such that I feel I have to make the position of our party perfectly clear. If I correctly remember what he said, and I took down his words, he made the statement that apparently we were co-operating with the government in order to get rid of parliament as soon as possible.
That is not the case, Mr. Speaker. We will be glad to co-operate with the government in doing what we can as members of the house to ensure that the house completes the business that the government puts before it with a minimum of delay, but without prejudice to our right and the right of every member of the house, on whatever side he may sit, to discuss fully, completely and thoroughly every measure that is submitted to the house. That is our responsibility, and we intend to discharge it. But within the limits of that responsibility we will co-operate in so far as we can to facilitate the business of the house.
However, Mr. Speaker, if that co-operation is to be of any value it is incumbent on the government, which has the responsibility, to organize the work of the session so that we can dispatch the business with a maximum of efficiency and a minimum of delay. That means that now, as we approach the period when we are trying to wind up the session, we should know what the business is for the rest of the session and where we stand in that regard. As we are discussing this matter today we have on the order paper for the first time, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Laurier a motion to establish a very important committee. We should therefore try to co-ordinate in the best way we can, perhaps through discussions among representatives of all three parties, not only the work of the house but the work of the committees. If we can do that perhaps we will be able to accomplish more than we otherwise would merely by passing this kind of motion.
My hon. friend has suggested to the Prime Minister, and I repeat the suggestion, that
4324	HOUSE OF
Business of the House
we would prefer to have the motion altered so that the longer hours of sitting, the diffi-cuties from which we all appreciate, will begin on Monday, June 6, instead of Wednesday, June 1. I put that suggestion to the Prime Minister. I hope he will feel it is possible to accept it. If he does, and if we can get together to organize the business of the session, which means that we must know now what that business is going to be, perhaps we will then be able to finish, although it certainly looks unlikely at the present time, some time around the middle of July. But if the Prime Minister and the government so desire, because it is their responsibility to make the decision, we will be prepared to adjourn and come back next autumn. Either of these courses is quite satisfactory from the point of view of the official opposition, but whatever course is adopted I hope we will know with the least possible delay what we are going to have before us for the remainder of the session.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
We should like, by this amendment, to put off as long as we can this undue rush which is contemplated in the initial motion presented by the Prime Minister. We have seen in other parliaments in Canada, notably in the province from which I come, British Columbia, this tendency to legislate by exhaustion. It may be that the same trend is developing here. The attitude of the government toward the introduction of items is that the time at which a measure is introduced is the prerogative of the government. They hold off the introduction or hold back the progress of items which are controversial and which require the greatest amount of consideration and research work to prepare for debate.
I have noticed this tendency during past sessions too, Mr. Speaker, and I am quite sure it is something that existed when the Liberal party was in office. They delay items of extreme importance to the country and to parliament until the latter part of the session, and make the introduction of these items coincide with the speed-up of the session, hoping thereby, as I said, to legislate by exhaustion. The members of the opposition, because of the fact that they are in opposition, have to do an extra amount of research and study, an extra amount of debate and discussion on these items as compared with government backbenchers who, generally speaking, do relatively little in this field. v
This motion, therefore, is for the convenience of the government, not for the convenience of parliament or as the result of concern over the effect these pieces of legislation will have on Canada. Certainly, I am quite sure, the Prime Minister would like to see his bill of rights introduced, debated and passed within one afternoon or within the shortest possible period of time. The item of business with which we will be dealing following the consideration of this motion is the amendment of the Combines Investigation Act. The Minister of Justice would like to see

this matter considered within the shortest possible time so the amendment can become law. There are other items such as the establishment of a forestry department and the amendment of the Civil Service Act, all of which are probably questions of major importance in this session, and this undue rush by attempting to keep parliament sitting morning, noon and night-I expect later on we will be sitting Saturdays, if past practice is followed-is designed so the government will meet the least amount of criticism during debate of the ideas which they propose.
The government knows full well it does not have to worry too much about undue criticism from members of its own party. It appears to be the traditional way government backbenchers function; that is, they place far more reliance in the government itself than they might if the government were formed by a different political party. Probably this is the normal course which government backbenchers follow.
The reasons for wanting to rush things at the end of the session were given by the government. They are looking toward completion of the work by July 1. If the government wanted to do something to ensure that its proposals received the fullest consideration, it could organize its activities in an orderly fashion in the early part of the session. The hon. member for Cariboo, who is sitting on the other side, is one member, for instance, who is extremely interested in a joint committee of this house and of the other place on Indian affairs. He is in regular attendance at the meetings of that committee. It is unfortunate, as practically every member of the committee has suggested, that we had to wait until the 44th day of this session before that particular committee was established. The committee on privileges and elections is in the same position. I am talking now, Mr. Speaker, about the conflict in time between the sittings of the committees and the sittings of the house, as well as the conflict between the sittings of various committees.
If the government had undertaken to speed up the progress of these items of extreme importance, we would not now be faced with additional conflicts in time and with the impossibility of not only trying to be in two places at the same time but in trying to be in three or four places at the same time. We can only come to the conclusion, because of the failure to proceed with these items at the proper time, that the government did not want detailed consideration to be given to these particular items.
I know full well that, so far as the general public are concerned, they generally could not care less whether parliament sits
Business of the House
six hours a day or eight hours or ten hours. Generally, this is a matter which does not enter into their consideration, because there are many people who are not even sure whether parliament is sitting. These are matters of extreme importance which will be of benefit to the whole of Canada, not for the benefit of members of parliament. The hon. member for Vancouver East set forth this argument very clearly and very succinctly. Naturally I endorse it. In any event, if our amendment is turned down, and it looks as though it is going to be, I do not think we should proceed with the initial motion which has been proposed.
I must apologize to you, sir, for getting off to a bad start by making reference to the frustration that develops amongst government backbenchers because of their inability or unwillingness to participate in debate, and who show their frustration in this way.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
It is a rather difficult position in which I find myself, Mr. Speaker, in following two or three of my colleagues in a debate of this kind. In their usual highly capable manner they have covered most of the points I had intended to use before they spoke. However, there are a few other points I should like to raise, and I should also like to underline a little more heavily some of the points with which they dealt.
There is much truth in the valid point raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I think this is something to which this house gives far too little consideration. I refer to the family responsibilities of the members of this house. I realize that in a country of this size it is perhaps impossible to work out a completely satisfactory arrangement as to whether hon. members should bring their families with them to Ottawa. I think that is a matter that should be given much greater consideration than it has been given in the past. On more than one occasion in the past extremely unfortunate developments have arisen because of the length of time the father is away from his children.
I think there is something else as well that should get more consideration than it has received in the past, namely the health of hon. members. This morning I attended the funeral of one who had been a member of this house. I should just like to bring to the attention of hon. members that this is the seventh hon. member who has passed on since the 1958 election. If we compare this situation to that of hon. members of the other place we find that although there is a great difference in age, to my knowledge at least

Business of the House
only one of the senators has passed on during that time. I think that is something we should consider when we are thinking about sitting extra hours and adding a further burden to hon. members of this house, with the consequent effect on their health.
I should like once more to underline just how much has been accomplished so far this session. We have passed the estimates of one department. A quick glance at the blue book shows that we have something in the neighbourhood of 37 more to pass before the session is concluded. Those estimates passed I believe total approximately $138,240,950. We still have something over $6 billion to pass before the session is over. What we have done so far we have been able to accomplish in about five months and, according to the Prime Minister, we hope to do all the rest in the next five weeks.
I do not see how this can be done, Mr. Speaker. I think it is an utter impossibility. If hon. members will stop for a moment and think, they will realize that if we carry on in that way, if we want to see our children this summer we had better bring them to Ottawa, because we shall be here until September.
Some complaint has been made in some of the newspapers that during this session we have had much sound and toy. That may be so. I am not making any remarks one way or the other on that matter. Possibly time has been used that could have been saved for some of the important business still left to be dealt with by this house. But the fact cannot be altered that the important business is still before this house, and it is going to have to be dealt with if members of this house are to carry out the responsibilities they accepted when they stood for office.
The hon. member for Skeena pointed out an extremely dangerous trend. It is one which I have noted is becoming more and more apparent each session that I have been down here. I refer to the fact that the important and possibly controversial legislation is always held up until the dying days of the session. I cannot blame the government for doing that. We would probably do the same thing if we were in their shoes; and if we did it they would probably do the same thing we are doing right now, namely criticize, and justifiably so.
To set a deadline of July 6, as we have heard suggested here, leaves only one choice to hon. members of this house. They either must abdicate their responsibilities in order to meet that deadline or they must jeopardize their health and practically kill themselves by working 24 hours a day. That is the only

way we can hope to accomplish the twofold job of concluding the session by July 5, 6, 7 or even July 30 and still give this legislation and these estimates the consideration that we were sent here to give them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JUNE 1
speechtext:
I should like to support the amendment suggesting that this motion do not become effective now but that it be delayed until July 1. I do that for the simple reason that most of us are sitting on committees. These committees are of importance or they would not have been named. A few months ago, when there was discussion on the setting up of one of these committees, it was pointed out that there was not any point in setting up these committees unless they were going to be able to do something. If we are going to be good opposition members there are certain things we must do. We are very few in number in the opposition; I refer to the total opposition. I want to claim no credit for that part of the opposition to which I do not belong, but in numbers the opposition are very small.
If we are going to start this rush movement I think we are going to be obliged to abdicate our positions on committees and do the work in the house. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this will amount to almost the same thing. If we wish to raise a matter, instead of doing so in committee we will raise it in the house on the estimates or in the appropriate place. I cannot see where this procedure is going to shorten the length of time the house sits.
Very shortly there will be a motion to extend the hours beyond ten o'clock at night, and to extend the sittings to include Saturdays. I am a young member. As far as I am concerned, if we want to have round the clock sittings that is perfectly all right; I will be here as much as anybody else during those sittings. But it seems to me that this is not a sensible system to follow. It is not the system used in other democratic countries. It is not the system used in Great Britain. It was decided there some time ago that a permanent arrangement would have to be made; that members of parliament were on a full time, year round basis. We are not sessional members of parliament, Mr. Speaker; we are members of parliament by the year, and we are expected to do a year's business.
I do not believe the country, when they made this concession, decided that they were going to allow the cabinet to run the government. I think the present Prime Minister is on the record many times as having said he did not like government run by order in council, and that he wanted government rim by parliament. Yet how is government being

run now? It is being run right off its feet. If the Prime Minister sat in this house as often as some of the other members, I suggest that he would be quite glad to cut down the hours rather than extend them because his health, and the health of other members, will not carry that kind of strain.
Just let us take a look at what happens in a committee of the House of Commons. We will go back just one week. These are the arrangements made, according to Votes and Proceedings:
Wednesday, May 25: public accounts committee, 9.30; joint committee on Indian affairs,
9.30	and 3.30; defence expenditures, 9.30.
Thursday: railways, canals and telegraphs,
9.30	and 3.00; privileges and elections, 9.30; joint committee on Indian affairs, 9.30 and 3.30.
Friday: agriculture and colonization, 9.30; defence expenditures, 9.30.
Monday: Mines, forest and waters, 11.00; estimates committee 11.00.
Tuesday: Mines, forests and waters, estimates-water resources; privileges and elections, the Canada Elections Act, both at 9.30.
Wednesday, June 1: public accounts, 9.30; defence expenditures, 9.30; joint committee on Indian affairs, 9.30 and 3.30.
I think it is ridiculous for us to have all these committees meeting. It may be advisable for the Canadian people to decide that they intend to change completely the form of government we have. It may be necessary to get rid of some of the things which may not serve as much purpose as looking after the estimates and certain other business. This might mean the elimination of the budget speech, the elimination of the throne speech and the elimination of some of the days which were set aside-the formal days-when the leaders on the front benches do the talking for two or three days at a time. It may be that hon. members themselves will need to give much closer consideration to the work they are sent here to do. Only now are we getting into the major committee work.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) went around this country during the last two or three years and said: I will set up a committee on anything that is important, and that committee will be given lots of responsibility, lots of scope; it will even be able to dabble in policy to some extent. That may be. But what will happen after the committee has made its report? We know what will happen. We will be putting our coats and hats on and leaving, because that will be the day when we prorogue. That will be the end of the session.
Business of the House
I have no objection to some of the western members going home and doing their farming. Unfortunately they had a bad year last year and some of them went home, not to put in the seed but to cut the grain. I would not mind that situation, because this house will run really effectively in the absence of 100 of the government's supporters. If that is what they want to do, I am all for them going home. I would not like to ask them to do something I would not like to do myself.
I accepted the job as member of parliament knowing full well the responsibilities that belong to the office, though I may not have known how much money I was going to get or what little distance it would' go. I knew it was a full-time job, and I expected that it would be a full-time job. If you are going to have young people run for parliament- people with young families, with children who are in school, then the time which would be most to their advantage would be the summer when they could take their families out to the lake. Goodness knows, the summer here in Canada is short enough, and if we were to decide to take July and August off we could probably enjoy the larger part of the summer.
There may be good reasons for some hon. members not wanting to sit here the year round. There may be-and I think there is- a really good chance of our doing the business that we do in six months much more effectively spread over the six months or a little longer. But how many things were on the order paper three weeks ago? How much legislation had already been introduced when 80 days of the session had gone by. I looked this up in order to do a radio broadcast, and found that very little legislation has been passed yet, while there was nothing of any importance on the order paper. When we asked the leader of the house not long ago what the business was going to be for the rest of the session he said: wait till the Prime Minister comes back from his conference in Europe, and we will sit down and decide how much of the legislation is still to come.
I have talked to some of the officials of the civil service. Maybe the government disagrees, but some of the members of the civil service association believe that amendments to the legislation governing the civil service are very important. They think that such amendments are worthy of a great deal of deliberation and discussion. What is going to happen is this: one morning we are going to find them on our desks. These amendments will be there, and we will be expected to approve them in the course of the afternoon. It will be something like the Combines Investigation Act. Yet it is a major piece of

Business of the House
legislation. When it is sent to the committee the committee will handle it for a week or so during the time when hon. members are supposed to be working on the estimates in the house. The committee will be discussing that which should have been discussed in the early part of the session.
If we are not sufficiently grown up in Canada to decide what we are going to do at the time when the government brings in the speech from the throne; if we cannot decide that and get it down at the beginning of the session, instead of playing around with tea parties and the other things we do during the first two or three days, we are not going to solve our difficulties by trying to do it in the last few days of a session. The government should have the ability to lay these things down on the order paper, and say: these are the important things: these are the things which are necessary for the well-being of the Canadian people; these are the things that are worthy of serious discussion; these are the things we recommend to the consideration of hon. members because they are important to the people they represent.
I may say, personally, that I do not see why we should not take a recess and come back in the fall. I can see no reason for not following that course. In Ontario they decided they were going to extend the school year. One can imagine what the children said about it. But you were probably surprised, Mr. Speaker, at what the teachers said about it. They said you could not extend the school year into the hot summer months and expect to get any more done than if you had taken those months off and come back refreshed.
I know exactly why the Prime Minister does not want to do this, and it is not because he is the least interested in his backbenchers. The reason he does not want to do it is because he thinks the opposition will get some backbone, that they will be told, when they get back to their ridings: why didn't you go after this, or why didn't you go after that; don't you know I am unemployed; don't you know I am not getting unemployment insurance, and so on. The opposition may come back with a stiffer backbone, and buckle down and go after some of the things we have already discussed. I agree that this might happen. It has happened before.
But I think if there were a little honesty between the government and those who sit on the front benches of the opposition, and the people they elect to represent them, then all those concerned could get together and work out some arrangement so that there would not be any undue repetition. It always appears to us that the whip is brought right down when we would like to go home,

too; advantage is taken of that situation, and everything is done as if we were working on a log boom somewhere.
It is quite true that if we came back in the fall there would probably be a little discussion on the unemployment situation. I believe there might be some talk of what the crops are doing in the west. There would, no doubt, be a little repetition of what the wheat problem is. But I think allowance should be made for these things. We could probably limit such debates to reviewing the situation. There would be no need for another speech from the throne, but some consideration should be given to these subjects.
I do not know whether the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) is going to introduce his bill on capital punishment again. He has been promised an opportunity, but I am sure he will be told: if you bring that in it is going to mean a whole day's debate-a whole day lost-and we would like to get away. However, that would not be very honest, because the Prime Minister told us in the house that there would be another day, and not a private members' day either, but a government day.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not want to interrupt relevant debate but it seems to me the hon. member is discussing almost every aspect of the business of the house. The matter before the house is whether this motion shall become effective June 1 or July 1. I suggest that the hon. member direct his attention to that question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Let us not tell the Canadian people we have been sitting idly by. Some hon. members are on 8 or 9 committees. We obviously cannot attend them all and if we are in the house we cannot attend any. We have passed only l/37th of the estimates. In another 20 days we may have passed another 20. We could then examine our position. We are not now anywhere near the end of the session. I could take 15 minutes to enumerate what has yet to be done. The work that is yet outstanding is of more public importance than what has been accomplished.
We ask that consideration of morning sittings be delayed until July 1. In the meantime the matter should be considered by the house leader. He should consider what he wants done and seek our co-operation. If the proposed course of action seems feasible we will co-operate but if not it is his obligation to suggest to the government that we recess and come back in the fall. If that were done the opposition could agree not to engage in a repetition of debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):

his seat. Which hon. member of his group could speak on behalf of the group with regard to such questions as the allocation of time for debate and so on?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I can speak on behalf of this group.
Oh, oh.

speechtext: The question is on the main motion. Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, after having listened very closely to the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) I hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) will agree as to the importance of committee and caucus meetings this week. Therefore I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin):
That the motion he amended by deleting therefrom the words "Wednesday, June 1", and substituting therefor "Monday, June 6".
I hope the Prime Minister will agree to this amendment.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-
Let the Speaker speak. He has already figured it out.
I submit to Your Honour that as the hon. member has spoken on the main motion by seconding the first amendment he is now precluded from again speaking and advancing another amendment.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam did not speak on the main motion but on the amendment. Therefore he is completely in order in speaking now. The hon. member for Edmonton West ought to sit down and think more before he rises.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question is whether an hon. member who submits a further amendment after having seconded an earlier amendment is in order in doing so. There is a ruling by the Speaker in the debates of 1952-53, page 1806, where the Speaker had this to say:
However, the rule also is to the effect that an hon. member who moves or seconds a subamendment and speaks, not only speaks to the subamendment but also speaks to the amendment. In the latter part of citation 293., I find these words:
"The mover and seconder of the amendment having spoken to the main question cannot speak again to it. The same rule applies, of course, to the case of an amendment to an amendment."
My ruling is that the hon. member for Assiniboia, having seconded the subamendment and having spoken to the subamendment, is prevented from speaking to the amendment. This does not, however, prevent other hon. members who have not spoken to the amendment from speaking to the amendment at this time. The hon. members who moved and seconded the subamendment along with the hon. member who moved the main amendment cannot speak at this time.
There is also a reference in Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 138. Paragraph 9 of citation 165 reads in part as follows:
The mover and seconder of the amendment having spoken to the main question cannot speak

Business of the House
again to it. The same rule applies, of course, to the case of an amendment to an amendment. The mover and seconder of an amendment are not penalized as compared with other members, because they speak both to the main question and the amendment which they are moving or seconding, in one speech.
The third paragraph of citation 165 reads as follows:
By moving or seconding an amendment a member, if he utters a few words, actually speaks to the main motion. It is only after the amendment has been put by the Speaker that it is considered a new question.
In the circumstances the amendment when offered by the hon. member seems to me to be out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I rise simply on a point of order at the moment, not to conclude the debate. So far as the government is concerned, I wish to say that when I speak I intend to accept the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition. I am not concluding the debate now.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express our appreciation to the Prime Minister. I had intended to move the same amendment but now it will not be necessary.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question? I must inform the house that if the Prime Minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to traverse the field that has been covered during the course of this debate. I do, however, wish to say immediately to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Ohevrier) that their attitude of co-operation in order to achieve the most effective operation of parliament is appreciated and in keeping with what one might expect from the hon. gentlemen with their regard for parliamentary procedure.
I think I should say a word too in respect of some of the remarks that came from the group to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker. I listened with interest to the statements of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who has had considerable experience in public life both in the House of Commons and in a provincial legislature. I found it somewhat difficult to understand some of those things to which he gave such high espousal today when considered in the light of some of the statements he has made in the past.
He spoke of parliament, the constitution and the necessity of maintaining parliament in all its amplitude, and with that I agree. There is nothing in this motion that interferes

in any way with the right of hon. members to speak to the fullest degree possible. The only thing it does is to give them more hours in which to place their views before the house.
As I listened to the hon. member I could not but recaU that on November 10, 1943 he brought before an audience he was addressing in the city of Calgary something of what the C.C.F. would do if they formed the government. To begin with, he said that they would scrap the British North America Act. That being so, Mr. Speaker, I can only believe that in the intervening years he has changed his views. He has never denied the accuracy of that statement. It was brought before parliament in his presence on one or two occasions and in fairness to him I can say there was no denial on his part then that he had in fact held those views and, indeed, there is nothing to indicate that he does not hold those views today.
Will the hon. member give the rest of that sentence?

I think that sentence is pretty well complete by itself. However, if the hon. member wants the rest of it I will give it. The hon. member said:
A change is coming, peacefully or not. When we become the government we will institute socialism immediately and would use the power of the police and the military forces to force those opposed to obey the law.
Oh, oh.
I had not intended to give the rest of the statement.
Just the same as you do today.

He went on to say:
Those who defied the government would be treated as criminals. If capitalism says "no" then we know the answer. So did Russia. We are going to scrap the B.N.A. Act.
Mr. Speaker, I was not going to cover that. I was dealing expressly with his views on parliament. As I listened to those views today I thought how different they were from those that he uttered on that occasion and also on subsequent occasions, but I do not have the record before me of those other occasions. Some offence was being committed against parliament. He said the attitude of the government and the official opposition is to get rid of parliament as soon as possible. It is nothing of the kind. There is nothing unusual in this motion.
Sometimes I find it difficult to know who speaks for that group of eight. One is the leader of the group in the house, and he spoke on this subject. I quote his words as an answer to those of his followers who spoke

today. On page 4238 of Hansard for June 2, 1959 the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) said:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is true to say that this is approximately the usual stage during a session when a motion is brought forward to provide for morning sittings.
As I pointed out when I introduced this motion, we are one day earlier on this occasion. I do not want to leave out anything the hon. member said. He went on to say this:
However, I do believe that at least some hon. members in this house are slightly in error in their thinking and in their hope that being a member of parliament is really just a part-time job. It seems to me that as the nation expands and parliament has to deal each session with an increasing volume of legislation, the fact becomes more and more clear that being a member is a full time job.
Then he goes on to say this:
In fairness I should also say that this motion to a substantial degree is a compromise motion. It is not a motion to call for morning sittings five days a week, nor does it call for evening sittings five days a week or on Saturdays. Instead it is asking that parliament sit Wednesday and Thursday mornings as well as Friday evenings in addition to the regular hours of sitting. At this particular stage of the session and in view of the attitude of the parties generally as to how sessions should be managed, we feel this is an appropriate time to bring forward a motion of this nature.
What has changed in one year? This is the appropriate time; that is what the house leader of that party, today absent on parliamentary business or absent from the house in any event, said one year ago. I accept, and the government of the day accepts, the views expressed last year in this regard by the leader of that party.
Then something was said regarding the necessity for having a planned session, and that the legislative program was not ready. May I say that the legislative program was ready when this house began its sessions. This was the course of action we determined upon last September. We placed the legislative program before parliament in exact proportion to the manner in which that program was being cleared off the order paper. This is not a question of a target date. In so far as I am concerned, I did say something about this on one occasion, and again I show that consistency which the eight expect from time to time.
I pointed out when I spoke in the house on March 11 that I had always been of the opinion that a divided session in one year was not in keeping with the tremendous responsibilities that rest on members, particularly in this country where members are so far from their homes and are unable to present their arguments as are members in 79951-0-273
Business of the House
the British House of Commons. I said, however, that if the legislative program dragged I might be forced to change my opinion. What was the attitude then? In an interview given by the house leader of the C.C.F. party, in absentia, outside the house, he said, "Reprehensible." Then he went on to say:
-if the government really is thinking of adopting the principle of dividing the sessions into winter, spring and fall sittings, there should be a conference among party leaders first.
Then he went on to say that such a suggestion on my part was a reprehensible one. What was reprehensible to the house leader in March has become the corner pillar of his followers in the month of June.
What is reprehensible about consultation?

Passing on from there, let me tell you this: The mother of parliaments is an example of the business-like and efficient conduct of parliament. I suggest this to you, Mr. Speaker, if one or two members in a small group in the British House of Commons decided that day by day they would hold up the legislative program placed before the house that would not be considered a proper or appropriate course. I need not identify what I have in mind. When eight hon. members decide that no matter what the rest of the house may consider proper and necessary with due regard to the full rights of the minority, they will delay legislation, then I ask them to read what has been repeatedly stated in that mother House of Commons in that regard.
Let me further say this, that parliament and the speed with which it shall discharge its responsibilities is not to be compared to a convoy, the speed of which is dependent upon the slowest ship. Over and over again this constant repetition is the measure of contribution to this House of Commons, not by quality but by quantity. I do not want in any way to prejudge the work of the committee on rules, but I am sure that the house will welcome suggestions from that committee which will ensure that parliament shall be able to advance and discharge its responsibilities, and carry out its legislative program in the most efficient and effective way.
May I say this, too: Some mention was made of certain measures that have yet to be considered. These measures will be placed before the house within the next day or so. In so far as the Civil Service Act and the Public Service Superannuation Act are concerned, they will be introduced within about a week. It is the government's intention to propose that the two bills be referred, after

Business of the House
second reading, to a special committee. This procedure will contribute to a more effective review of the measures, and I think expedite proceedings of the house.

When does the committee
meet?
After all, the legislation has to be introduced and then a determination will be made as to the time and place of that committee meeting.
I was not thinking of that. I was thinking that it will meet at 11 o'clock every morning, the same time as the house.

As the hon. member well knows from that knowledge of parliamentary government to which I have already paid such warm tribute, the committee will make that decision.
It is well to look over the record of the committees this session. I think the hon. member for Vancouver East has said that they have done well; at least, that is my recollection. The committees that have met and have finished their work are the external affairs committee; the estimates committee; the railways, airlines and shipping committee; the standing orders committee; veterans affairs committee; marine and fisheries committee and the committee on industrial relations. The committee on privileges and elections should be finished by June 7.
With regard to the future legislative program, may I say this? Further to the items already on the order paper will be the bill of rights. The Leader of the Opposition asked me particularly whether it will be submitted to a committee of the house. That is the purpose following second reading. Then there is the Russian trade treaty, the setting up of the department of forestry, the C.N.R. financing bill and the three budget bills. In addition to those I have named there will, of course, be the Civil Service Act and the Public Service Superannuation Act. As to other matters of legislation, as I have said, the house will be advised thereof within the next day or so.
Again in accepting the suggestion amending the motion as moved, may I say that our purpose must always be to make this chamber efficient and effective. No target date has been set. I expressed the hope that if each hon. member would make his contribution on the basis of providing the fullest and most complete examination of the legislation that is brought before parliament- if even that were done-my expectation was that we would be in a position to prorogue at that time. However, hon. gentlemen tell me that is not so, that that objective cannot

be achieved. I will not argue with them. The house will determine that matter. If it is the desire to continue beyond that date-and I have set that as an objective that all of us would work to-I have no argument about the matter. I simply say this. The legislative program that is before the house, or is to be introduced, will require to be given attention and before the conclusion of the session will, I hope, have received the support and commendation of this house.
Before I conclude there is one other matter to which I want to make an allusion. I agree most wholeheartedly that we in this house must maintain strictly the proprieties in debate. No action must be taken on the part of anyone and no word must be spoken that conveys the suggestion that any hon. member has not the full right to speak as he will, provided he does so within the rules. I am not here in the position of condemning anyone. However, today during the course of his remarks the hon. member for Vancouver East made the suggestion that somebody had told him to shut up.
Did you not hear it?

I made an examination to see what actually took place. My examination shows this, and I think the record will show it; I have written down the notes in that regard. During his remarks the hon. gentleman said this: "If this house is to meet at eleven o'clock on Monday through Friday, then I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how does an ordinary member take care of his work on a constituency basis; how does he find time to attend to grievances, attend committees and attend the House of Commons at the same time?"
The hon. gentleman was asking for information. He was craving an answer to that question. He found himself in a difficult position, Mr. Speaker. He found that he could not trifurcate himself, as it were, so he asked a natural question: how does one find time to attend to grievances, attend committees and attend the House of Commons at the same time? Then he started to answer his own question and he was helped.
What he said was this: there is only one thing a member can do on that basis. We shall never know, Mr. Speaker, what answer the hon. gentleman was going to give to his own question but somebody answered "that is, shut up".
I would be the first to take the strongest objection to anyone directing that admonition to any hon. member. But I am sure that on reflection the hon. member for Vancouver East with his parliamentary experience, long

and effective as it has been, to that extent will agree that when you ask a question you sometimes get an answer.
Mr. Speaker, I never thought-
Order.
-that the Prime Minister could get that small.

It was on a question of privilege but I am sorry that the Prime Minister is not worthy of that much attention.
Before the motion is put, will the Prime Minister answer a question arising out of his remarks?
Yes.

When he referred to the legislation pertaining to the civil service and the sending of it to a committee after second reading did he anticipate that that legislation would be dealt with at all stages by the committee and returned to the house and be dealt with before the termination of this session of parliament which he indicated he thought would be by June 30?

I should like to rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister indicated that he had had a look at the words of the hon. member for Vancouver East.
