subtopic: LATIN AMERICA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON VISIT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in order to expedite matters I will ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he has a report to make on his recent trip to Latin America, and more particularly whether he has anything to say on the possibility of Canada's association with the organization of American states?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LATIN AMERICA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON VISIT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to that question, perhaps the house will excuse me if I take a few minutes to give a short report of my trip. The purpose, of course, was to attend the celebrations commemorating 150 years of independence of Argentina and also while in South America to pay brief visits to Chile and Peru.
Roughly speaking, I had in mind furthering the good will between Canada and the Latin American countries and also endeavouring to learn something about our southern neighbours.
I must say at once that I was very much impressed by all those countries which I had the good fortune to visit. Argentina is, I found, very similar to Canada. Of course, they have ranches producing wheat and cattle. They have the great port of Buenos Aires, one of the main ports of the world, and also they are active in the Antarctic just as we are in the Arctic. The population is slightly larger than that of Canada. Argentina ranks in the world today as a middle power, in the same status as our own nation.
There I had a very helpful conference with the president of Argentina and the foreign minister. In fact I had two with the foreign minister, having been invited to dinner at the Brazilian embassy with him by the foreign minister of Brazil, Hon. Mr. Lafer, who made such a friendly visit here a few months ago.
Argentina had over 80 delegations visiting the country for this celebration. That did not mean 80 foreign ministers; of course all the

Inquiries of the Ministry heads of delegations were not foreign ministers. It meant that they were entertaining five or ten times as many as 80, which is quite a big exercise, and they did it in an extremely efficient and friendly way. I think it did them great credit.
Of course one had opportunities for meetings and discussions with other representatives, other foreign ministers and other ministers and heads of delegations from various countries. As I pointed out a moment ago, I had more than one occasion for discussions with Mr. Lafer, of Brazil.
There were, of course, many important events. One was the celebration of the Te Deum in the cathedral of Buenos Aires, which was a most impressive ceremony. A state dinner was given by the president and there was a military parade which took four hours to pass and which was extremely good. I was very much impressed by the young men of Argentina who participated in it. There were men not only from the navy but also they have marines; infantry and also paratroops, ski troops for the Antarctic and mountain troops for the Andes. They have a very impressive force. Also participating were small forces from the neighbouring countries and, significantly, forces from Spain were given the place of honour at the head of the parade.
In Buenos Aires they have one of the finest theatres in the world. It ranks, I think, as the third best in the world. There was an excellent ballet performance one evening with ballet companies from Paris, Buenos Aires and London.
There was one visit I paid which might be of interest to hon. members. It was to a school in Buenos Aires. They have two schools there, one elementary and one secondary, which are named Canada schools. I visited one of those schools. It was a holiday but the children had all been brought out to meet the foreign minister from Canada, and that was quite a test. I did not find out this was happening until the children had all gone home. There they were. They all wore white smocks, both the boys and the girls. They had a Canadian flag and the flag of Argentina. They sang songs and a very nice speech was made by one of the teachers but as it was in Spanish I did not get the full drift of it. In any event, this was a very wonderful lesson to me with respect to the way in which good will can be spread among the nations.
When I was speaking to the youngsters afterward I asked the girls whether their mothers washed their smocks or whether they did and they admitted that their mothers did. I said, "Don't you think that is terrible?


Why don't you do it yourselves?" One little girl looked at me and said, "Who washes the smocks in Canada?" This had me floored and they laughed at that. One of these schools is affiliated with a school in Toronto and I am hoping that a secondary school will be affiliated with a high school in the remarkable riding of Vancouver Quadra. Other schools are named after other countries. Our ambassador is helping by getting reading material to these schools and to further understanding the children are supposed to write to children in Canada and vice versa.
In Chile I found great tragedy. I visited the minister of the interior who is in charge of the relief measures. He told me they had over 500,000 people homeless in the stricken area, and with winter coming on and the season of heavy rain the whole situation is very serious for them. I also visited the minister of finance and the acting minister of foreign affairs. It will cost at least half a billion dollars to repair the damage that has been done. Roads have been destroyed. Homes, public buildings, wharves and harbours have been destroyed. They do not know what has happened to the harbours. Much of the shoreline in that part of Chile has been changed. New islands have come up out of the sea and old islands have been submerged. There are also four new volcanoes.
All this has happened in one of the country's very best regions, a district where they have their only steel plant and their only pulp and paper plant. People in the capital of Santiago could not get word of what had happened to their relatives in the earthquake zone. People were sitting outside the office of the minister of the interior trying to find out something about their relatives. We saw quite a few trucks heading south with bedding and all sorts of materials for the people there. On the airfield at Santiago there were huge United States Globemasters. The United States at once flew two large mobile hospitals to Chile, these hospitals having over 250 beds each. Not only did I see Globe-masters at Santiago but there was also another at Antofagasta on my way north and at Lima, Peru, there were two or three more. From all over the world help was coming for these people.
The people of Chile have shown remarkable courage. The ministers were under terrific pressure, of course and had been working day and night. Disaster struck the country just when it was recovering from a very difficult period economically. They do not know how they will bring about rehabilitation under these conditions. This is the worst disaster they have ever suffered but I am sure that every Canadian, if he could be

there, would admire the way in which the people of Chile are facing this tragedy.
Last Saturday night, I believe, 10 cases of clothing were shipped from Vancouver by the Canadian Red Cross through the courtesy of Canadian Pacific Air Lines. Forty-eight cases of new, not used, clothing as well as medicines have also been sent to Chile by our Red Cross.
One of the most urgent requirements was for mobile hospitals of a smaller size. The large United States mobile hospitals were very helpful but it was difficult to get the injured people to the large centres. So the Chilean minister of the interior asked if we could send a small mobile field hospital. Through the co-operation of the departments of national defence and national health and welfare complete medical equipment for a 30-bed field hospital, together with 40 stretchers, 160 blankets and extra instruments and dressings, was dispatched Saturday afternoon and will be in Santiago tomorrow. In addition, 50,000 water sterilization tablets, 10,000 penicillin and 10,000 tetracycline tablets and 40 pounds of refrigerated antitetanus toxoid and tetanus vaccine were also sent.
I think further help will be needed and provision has been made for some help in the way of food. The minister asked for flour and canned meats and 1 million pounds of canned pork has now been turned over to the Gold Cross by the Department of Agriculture and will be forwarded without cost to Chile. This pork is worth $600,000. We shall be doing what we can to help in this very tragic situation and it may be that we will have to ask the house for authority to give further assistance. The Chileans were deeply grateful for help and, as I have said, help is coming from all over the world. This is one of the great disasters of our time.
I flew up the coast to Lima, Peru, on Friday afternoon. Lima was the seat of the viceroy in the old Spanish days. It is a city of over a million people, as in Santiago; and Buenos Aires, of course, has between four and five million people. In Lima I had conferences with the president and with the prime minister. I met him on two occasions and had very useful talks with him. He has been in Canada and the United States and is doing an outstanding job. He is the owner of La Prensa, one of the leading papers in Lima. Incidentally, I also met Dr. Gain Za Pas, the owner of La Prensa in Argentina. Both of these men have suffered for freedom of the press. Dr. Gain Za Pas, as you know, fled Argentina a few years ago. His actions have been hailed all over the world and, of course,
Inquiries of the Ministry from coast to coast in Canada. The prime minister of Peru was in jail at one time because of the views he had put forward in his paper.
On Saturday afternoon we had a reception for Canadians in Lima. The delegation received an exceedingly warm welcome there as we did in each of the other places we visited.
In Mexico City yesterday I was met at the airport by Hon. Mr. Tello, the foreign minister. We had a very helpful talk. He drove me to the University of Mexico which has 50,000 students and provides a good objective for Canadian universities in the way of buildings and developments of that type.
On the way down we landed for gas at Brasilia. It was planned to go to Rio which we did eventually but at that time it was fogged in and we landed first at Brasilia. This is the most impressive development I have ever seen. I had read a great deal about it but that is different from actually seeing this brand new capital carved out of the woods, with huge apartment buildings and government buildings that must have cost a great many millions of dollars. It will be a wonderful capital and it means so much to the people of Brazil as a symbol of their development and of the great nation they have become.
In all these countries our Canadian ambassadors and their staffs are doing a splendid job for Canada. In a very real way, they are in the front line in our relations with other countries, and I found them all doing a splendid job.
All of these countries are very much interested in Canada. They are very friendly. Their outlook on world affairs is very much the same as our own. They place great value on their independence. They are all strong supporters of the United Nations and, as a matter of fact, each one of them has had a president of the United Nations, that is, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru and Mexico. I think one of them has had two presidents of the United Nations. Canada has always enjoyed the co-operation of these countries in the United Nations, but they are deeply puzzled that Canadians do not seem to realize that Canada is a very important member of the western hemisphere family. I met this attitude everywhere I went, just a little feeling that Canadians are of the opinion they do not want to be too much involved with these Latin American nations.
I can only say to the house that each one of these countries would make a very staunch friend of Canada. They are all playing a very important part in world affairs, and they are steadily growing in stature. I believe

Inquiries of the Ministry it will not be very many years until there are more people south of the Rio Grande than there are north of it. I think that Latin America is on the move. These nations, as I have said, are very much like our own, and I believe are extremely important to Canada.
I cannot go farther than that with regard to Canadian policy at the moment. I do say this, however, that the policy of the government has been and is to further improve the good relations which exist between Canada and the Latin American nations. For example 9 plan to set up in the department of external affairs a Latin American division. At the present time we only have a subdivision dealing with Latin American business, but it is far too important to be treated in that way. We have very much in mind the need for closer co-operation with these western hemisphere neighbours of ours and steps will be taken toward that end.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I appreciate very much indeed the courtesy which the house showed me just before six o'clock this evening.
In discussing the position and the policy of the government in connection with the bill
4340	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act now before the house-Bill No. C-58 to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code-I should like to make it clear that what we have presented to the house are amendments to the combines legislation, not a general revision. I know there have been suggestions from time to time that there should be a general revision of the legislation in this field, but it is my view-and it is shared by my colleagues, and I think it will be shared by the house and the country generally-that a general revision would require, possibly, a royal commission and at least a study of the principles of the legislation by a parliamentary committee-a far-reaching and important study beyond the scope of the study we have given to the matter so far and certainly beyond the scope of the amendments which are introduced here tonight.
I should like, therefore, to make it clear that the bill, whose second reading I now move, proceeds on the basis of the inherent soundness of the principles of the present anti-combines legislation. I shall have more to say later with regard to my own view as to the principles of that legislation, and I shall have something to say also with regard to the particular application of those principles. However, I do wish to emphasize that the bill before the house is framed and presented within the general ambit of the principles of combines legislation as we now have it.
In this connection, and in the light of some of the comments which appeared in the press with regard to the bill both this year and last year, perhaps I may be permitted to remind the house that the first anti-combines legislation in Canada was introduced by a Conservative government in 1889. It antedated by one year the introduction of the first federal anti-combines legislation in the United States which, I believe, was the Sherman act.
In 1889, as a result of a committee study, a private member introduced a bill which was later taken over by the government of the day. It was moved by Sir John Thompson, the then minister of justice, that the order be transferred from public bills and orders to government orders. It was then put through as a government measure. That act was followed in 1892 by a further piece of amending legislation introduced on that occasion by the government of which Sir John Thompson was then prime minister, containing in essence the definition of a combine and the essential provisions under which combines were outlawed; provisions which are still contained, with only minor alterations, in the


Criminal Code of today in that very important section of the code under which over the years the great majority of combines charges have been laid and prosecuted.
I mention this in order that we may get the whole discussion into perspective, because there have been many suggestions over the years that the governments formed by the party of which I have the honour of being a member have been opposed to combine legislation, and that today we are attempting to do something to weaken the central theme and the operative effect of this legislation. It is, I feel, important that I should give this piece of background in order to remind the house that both the enactment and the amendment-the bringing up to date of anti-combines legislation-is completely in accord with the position of the Conservative party and of Conservative governments over the years, that position being one of belief in the protection of the general interest of society against special interests.
However, this position is based on a fundamental principle that legislation must be workable and practicable and must be kept in touch with the movement of the times. The effect and intention of legislation must be clear, both in order that those who are affected by it may know what their position is, and in order that another very important principle may be maintained, namely that it should not be the government which from day to day determines by private decision what are the rules governing business and society generally, but that the rules governing business and society should be laid down in legislation which speaks clearly and which is capable of fair and immediate application. It is in this spirit and with this traditional background that this government introduces the present amendment to the combines legislation.
While I want to make it clear that the amendments do proceed within the ambit of the principles of the present provisions, we have felt, and do feel, that there are a number of improvements which could be made to the act as it exists. It was with this feeling in mind that immediately upon assuming office with the approval of my colleagues I commenced a study of the combines legislation within my department.
This study was carried out in conjunction with the advisers of my department and of the combines investigation branch, as well as with representatives of business and business organizations who lost no time in making representations to us. It was also carried out in conjunction with organizations representing small businesses and with many other organizations representing every variety of

interests throughout the country. I should like to express my appreciation, and that of the government of Canada, for the contribution which was made by all these organizations and individuals in taking the time and the trouble to bring their views before us and to make constructive and helpful suggestions with regard to the present legislation.
These discussions have been continuing since the time we assumed office in June of 1957 and they have been full and detailed. As a result of these discussions we came to the conclusion that our feeling that there should be and could be improvements to the present legislation were entirely justified.
It was our conclusion that the room for improvement lies in two main areas. The first is in the field of combines legislation as it affects small business. The second is in the field of general improvement.
As to the first, I should like to remind the house of the consistent philosophy of Conservative governments with regard to the problems of small business and small businessmen. I shall have more to say about this in detail later but I just lay the groundwork now by the statement that in general this government believes and Conservative governments have believed over the years that the best and soundest economy is that economy which is based upon the maximum participation of the greatest possible number of independent operators in that economy, and that it is an unsound economy which relies for its operations either on the employment of everybody by the government or the employment of everybody by some giant corporation or corporations. Our objective, therefore, and our philosophy in this field is to bring the maximum reconciliation in the way of the protection of small businessmen, on the one hand, and the interests of the community, of the consumers and of society generally on the other.
I should perhaps remind the house here that our interest in the welfare of small business is demonstrated not only by the amendments which we are introducing to the combines legislation at the present time as a result of those studies which we have made, but also by the establishment a year or so ago, in accordance with a previous pledge, of the small business section of the Department of Trade and Commerce which has been working quietly and effectively with the representatives of small business and small businessmen to devise policies which would protect and promote the interests of the small independent operators.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, in what I am saying that this is a consistent policy adopted
79951-0-274J
Combines Investigation Act by this government and this party over the years. I am sure that many hon. members in the house today will remember the position we took in 1951 when there was before parliament an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act which resulted in the enactment of the present section 34 of that act. At that time the position taken by the Conservative party, then in opposition, was that the legislation was hasty and ill conceived because, although based upon a principle which in theory commanded some popular support and indeed some general support, it was enacted at a time and in a manner which left small business completely defenceless against the operation of their more powerful competitors and the large chain concerns and particularly which left them defenceless against that practice known as loss leader selling as well as a variety of other types of unfair competition.
It was on that basis that we took our position in opposition to the enactment of section 34 in 1951-on the basis that while we would not condemn the principle that manufacturers should not have the right to impose their own price structure throughout the whole chain of distribution and retail selling, nevertheless the legislation of that day left the small businessman defenceless against the evils to which we anticipated he would be exposed. Our fears were substantiated and have been substantiated by the experience of small business over the years since that time. Particularly they were substantiated by the complaints and representations that I received during the months and years within which, as I have outlined to the house, our study of this legislation has been carried on since we assumed office in June of 1957.
As a result of the consideration of the representations that were made to us we came to the conclusion that we would be justified and that indeed it was essential that we amend section 34 of the Combines Investigation Act to give a measure of protection to the small businessman. We came to the conclusion that we would not be justified in repealing the section and we made that clear to those with whom we discussed it from the very outset but we said we did believe their position required protection and that we would study and consider the introduction of amendments to the section to give them some degree of protection to which they were legitimately entitled.
The second of the two main fields in which we came to the conclusion that improvements to the combines legislation could and should be made was in the area of bringing up to date and clarifying the law so as to make it more adaptable to the mid-twentieth

Combines Investigation Act century economy in which Canada, Canadian business and the national economy must exist and compete.
I want to emphasize for a moment that in a country such as Canada with an economy dependent as it is on successful competition in international as well as domestic markets it is essential that this type of legislation with which we are dealing, the anti-combines legislation, should take account of the type of economic climate in which the nation exists. It is not my purpose either at this time or at any time during the discussion of the legislation which I have the honour to present to enter a plea for or against business or individual businessmen as such. I rather base my position on what I believe to be a realistic assessment of the position of the Canadian economy generally. I do suggest, however, it is an essential fact for us to realize that the Canadian economy depends in very large measure upon the success of Canadian business and the welfare of the Canadian worker depends to a very large extent, as does the ability of the Canadian government to meet its responsibilities, upon the welfare of Canadian business.
I think this can and should be said but certainly in saying it-and I emphasize this -I am not entering a plea for or against the individual position of any particular business or businessman. In the light of this- what I take to be a reasonably self-evident fact with which I doubt if my hon. friends in the opposition will quarrel; in the light of this proposition-I am somewhat surprised to find the lengths to which certain newspapers, new organs,-generally speaking, those which support the party to which my hon. friends in the official opposition belong-have gone in discussing this legislation. I am somewhat surprised to find the virulence of their attack upon Canadian business. I make this comment merely by way of general comment because I am quite certain that you, Mr. Speaker, and other hon. members of this house and members of the public outside this house will have read some of those articles. I do not think that at the present time, at any rate, I need to go any further than to make the general comment because it is my view, that the very virulence and violence of those attacks destroy their effectiveness.
However, I shall come back later to this question of the general philosophy which should govern the attitude toward the various people affected by the combines legislation when I discuss some particular changes we are making. At the moment, however, I was making the point that we are living in the mid-twentieth century, and the laws by which

we govern-and those laws include the government and welfare of individuals as well as business-must keep pace with the economic developments of the times. It is in part in that spirit that we have approached the problems of amending the combines legislation.
As I say, as a result of our studies we came to the conclusion that there could be improvements made in the law in the light of those considerations. We came to the conclusion that there are uncertainties in the law and that, as a result of those uncertainties, there have arisen rigidities in the patterns and in the attitudes of business itself. It is as a result of those rigidities, which in turn arise from the uncertainties with regard to the law, that some practices are discouraged-not practices which might be but practices which would be beneficial in their results to society-simply because of the uncertainties which exist in the minds of those concerned with regard to the provisions of the law and their general extent and effect.
It seemed to us that it is a responsibility of the government in reviewing the law and in the circumstances under which we reviewed it that, having come to this conclusion, we should take what steps we could to remove those uncertainties in order that we might make it possible-not dictate, because we do not dictate either to the individual or to business-but make it possible that those practices which would be beneficial to the economy might be carried out, and we believe will be carried out, by business when those uncertainties are removed.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that in the particular field of combines legislation-I am here dealing with combines as a technical term as distinguished from mergers and monopolies-we came to the conclusion that what is called the per se rule should be retained and maintained in its full vigour and effect. I want to state here and to make clear beyond the bounds of controversy-and I shall be restating it from time to time in the course of this discussion-that with regard to a combination in restraint of trade which has for instance the elements of price fixing or the parcelling up of markets, or the prevention of entry into the field by other individuals or enterprises, there is no weakening, no lessening in our position of condemnation of that kind of operation. And by the same token and to the same extent there is no weakening, no lessening, no cutting away of the foundation of the legislation or of the case law which condemns such operations under what I have called the per se rule, which is the result of the application of judicial decisions to the legislation and which has in effect laid down

the policy that such combinations are offences per se. There is no weakening of this principle but, Mr. Speaker, within this framework we believe that clarity and improvement could be achieved even in that branch of the law which relates to combines as distinct from mergers and monopolies.
And so as the result of this process of study and discussion, we came to the conclusion that legislation should be introduced having as its end three main purposes: first, the consolidation of the existing provisions of the anti-combines legislation; second, the clarification of those provisions; and, third, the provision of new procedures and remedies open to the government, procedures and remedies by which the combines branch and my department may more readily enforce the law in the interests of society generally.
It is, I think, interesting, and it is appropriate for me to point out at this time, that two of those three headings which I have mentioned as main purposes of the legislation, namely consolidation, and provision of new procedures, are covered by the recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee which was appointed by our predecessors, and whose report is found in the volume entitled, "Report of the committee to study combines legislation" printed in 1952. I would refer the house particularly to page 37, pages 40 to 41 and page 48 of that report as the foundation for the statement I made that two out of those three purposes are included in and supported by the report of the MacQuarrie committee.
Within that general background, Mr. Speaker, may I turn to the history of the amendments before the house. You will remember that during the course of the last session the government introduced a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code with the purposes as I have mentioned in mind. That bill was No. C-59. It is interesting, Mr. Speaker-and I know I must not revive a debate-to recall, in the light of what was said this afternoon that this year we seem to be one stage ahead because the bill we have this year is No. C-58. To that extent the house is better off than perhaps some of my hon. friends were suggesting during the course of this afternoon.
After the introduction of that bill we received representations from businessmen, retail merchants associations, professional economists, consumer and other groups, that the bill should be deferred so that those groups might have an opportunity to study it more thoroughly and make representations to us about it. In view of the importance of legislation of this kind for the welfare of our whole economy we considered it our duty to
Combines Investigation Act ensure that the legislation which would ultimately be enacted would be in the most adequate, effective and workable form. We accordingly decided to postpone until this session the consideration of such amendments to the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code.
At that time I declared that while the bill might not be in exactly the same form as the one introduced last year, it was our firm intention to reintroduce legislation along the same lines at the present session and to deal with that legislation at this session. As a result, we received a large number of representations from various organizations and people representing all sections of the community. I should like once again to express my appreciation to all those who have made representations for the assistance they have given in the study which we felt should be made of the legislation which we proposed to introduce, which study has been carried on again in great detail since last year.
The result of this study is the bill which was introduced in this house on May 6 and is now before us. In reading this bill, hon. members will, I know, have noticed that it embodies some modifications from last year's proposed amendments, and also some new provisions which did not appear in the previous bill and perhaps, for convenience of reference and discussion, I might be permitted to divide the provisions of the present bill into three main groups.
First, there is the set of substantive amendments, amendments affecting the offences as they are spelled out in the law. These are, in short, the amendment of the provisions relating to conspiracy and several amendments in the matter of unfair trade practices, especially in relation to the operations of small businesses.
Second, there is a set of what could be called procedural amendments. They relate in particular to the new jurisdiction conferred on the Exchequer Court of Canada, an amendment permitting a restraining or dissolution order without a conviction where the offence has been completed; also, a provision requiring the commission to make certain additional specific findings where it appears that a combine has existed.
Next in this group are the amendments consolidating the related provisions of the Criminal Code and the Combines Investigation Act and ensuring the uninterrupted continuation of the law contained in section 411 of the Criminal Code.
Third, there is a group of what I would call consequential amendments. These are represented in particular by restatements of

Combines Investigation Act definitions made necessary as a result of consolidation of the legislation, and a certain number of amendments dealing with changes in the cross-references. I should like to emphasize at this point, Mr. Speaker, that although there have been restatements of definitions made necessary as a result of consolidation there has been no change in the effect of the definitions. We have been as careful as we could be to make certain that, although we were carrying out the rewording made necessary by these consolidations, there was no change in the effect and that the only change that was made was along the lines of greater clarification.
Having summarized the nature and groupings of the amendments, perhaps I should proceed now to a brief discussion of the principles behind the anti-combines legislation because I think it is important to emphasize again that the principles behind these amendments are the fundamental principles so far contained in Canadian anti-combines legislation. I should also like at this point to come to the discussion which I forecast, namely a discussion of the government's position with relation to those principles.
As I have previously indicated, the government believes that the principles of the legislation now in effect are sound, and it could hardly be otherwise inasmuch as I may perhaps be permitted to remind the house again that it was a Conservative government which first introduced the main operative provision of the anti-combines legislation. What are these principles? I think it should be recalled by the house that the Canadian legislation in this field is of very long standing. As I have pointed out, the first provision in our history antedates by one year the first federal provision in the United States. All through these years the principle at the basis of the 1889 act has been constantly maintained by parliament. We find that principle in the present Combines Investigation Act; and in the proposed amendments before the house it is maintained in its full integrity.
The basic principle is that a free enterprise system is the system which will yield the highest material standard of living in conjunction with the greatest possible degree of political, economic and social freedom for the individual and that this system of free enterprise will be best maintained through the operation and preservation of active competition between the various sectors of the economy. It is our belief that in most sectors of society competition is still the best mechanism for allocating resources and distributing what those resources produce and for regulating relationships between men in the course of production and consumption.

We reject on the one hand the rigid and unfair system of a cartelized economy whereby huge industrial concerns and financial empires would completely control the destinies of the economy and in the end the affairs of our society. We categorically refuse such a system of allocation of resources, relying as it must upon the mechanism of monopolies and combines and other similar trade and industry arrangements. But we also reject on the other hand the paraphernalia of state planning, a system of state regimentation whereby the government would make deliberate decisions as to the amount of resources that would be allocated to each of the different needs of the community and where the government would determine not only the conditions and quantities of production but also, of course, the price and the quality of the product, and would also have to determine and dictate who and how many people would engage and where they would engage in the production, the distribution and the retailing of the particular product.
We as the government, Mr. Speaker, do not want business to take over government but neither do we want the government to take over business. What we want, to the greatest extent possible, is a free enterprise system according to which the allocation and distribution of resources will be determined by the operation of active competition, and this is where the anti-combines legislation comes into the picture. This legislation is a program designed to maintain those competitive conditions which will make a free enterprise system work and work to the advantage of society and all segments of that society.
In order to achieve that purpose the anticombines legislation, however, must deal with various types of situations, price fixing combines, mergers, monopolies and various unfair trade practices. It is thus apparent that there must be two main groups of provisions found in any effective anti-combines legislation and these two main groups of provisions are found in the Canadian anti-combines legislation. The principles of these provisions are accepted by the government in accordance with the philosophy I have just outlined, and it is on the basis of those principles that we have brought in this bill to improve, modernize and make more effective the machinery by which these principles are carried into practice.
Perhaps at this point I should elaborate in somewhat greater detail what are the concepts and effects of these two main groups of provisions. The first group is that group dealing with combinations, mergers and monopolies. The purpose and effect of this

group of provisions are to protect the interests of society in free competition, to protect that interest against the temptations, the pressures if you like, to which business, if left free to its own devices, would be exposed and subjected, pressures and temptations which would and on occasion have led them into the pattern of combination, merger or monopoly.
The second main group of provisions is a group dealing with specific unfair trade practices. The purpose of this group of provisions, as contrasted with the first group, is to bring a degree of protection, particularly for small businesses, against the power of the purse and the danger that such small businesses will be eliminated not because in their own field they are inefficient but simply because they do not command the size and weight of resources which their competitors command and which resources can be used ruthlessly or unfairly to eliminate their smaller competitors.
In protecting thus, in specific detail if you like, the position primarily of the smaller businessmen and smaller businesses we are, I submit, also protecting society itself because, as I have indicated previously, it is our view that society also has an interest in seeing to it that the maximum number of independent businesses consistent with efficiency are kept in operation.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Consistent with efficiency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
We believe, as I have said before, that that economy is in the soundest condition which is based upon the participation of the maximum number of independent operators. I heard somebody on the other side say "consistent with efficiency", thereby picking up a remark that I had made. May I remind the house that in the same way as we believe that bigness is not necessarily badness, notwithstanding what some of the newspapers have said, so we also believe that bigness is not necessarily synonymous with efficiency, and it is our view that there are just as efficient operators in the field of small business as there are in the field of big business. It is our desire and our aim in this legislation to protect these efficient small operators against the power of the purse which is sometimes brought against them ruthlessly and unfairly by very large and powerful competitors.
And so, Mr. Speaker, this bill starts from these basic assumptions I have outlined and proceeds on the basis that there are, and should be, these two main groups of provisions. On this basic assumption, the bill seeks to accomplish two things. First, it is
Combines Investigation Act designed to improve the existing provisions of the legislation by way of clarification and consolidation and, second, it is designed to bring the law in important particulars into line with twentieth century developments and to adapt it to the problems and situations of the twentieth century economy.
On the basis of this classification of the provisions into two main groups, may I offer first an analysis of the amendments. Among those amendments conducive to the first objective I would suggest the following: The consolidation of the Criminal Code and the Combines Investigation Act provisions; the clarification and consolidation of the definition sections-again emphasizing that there is no change in effect; the provision making it clear that acts which are beneficial to the public, such as the pooling of resources for research and do not constitute a combine as defined can be carried on without danger of mis-construction or conviction.
Among the amendments conducive to the second objective, for instance, are those such as the provision to protect the small businessman against discriminatory and unfair trade and pricing practices; the provision against misleading advertising; the provision-with respect to this one I must say that to some extent it promotes both the first and second objectives-to establish that various types of co-operative activity which are beneficial can be carried on. Again, I mention the type of activity which is embraced within the provision regarding the pooling of resources for research.
Perhaps I should stop here for a moment to mention one of the submissions that was made to us and which, quite frankly, carried a very great deal of weight with us. It is a statement of fact that in comparison with United States industries Canadian industries are at a great disadvantage. One can think of almost any number-certainly a considerable number-of United States industries which would embrace within the single scope of their activities the market and the productive capacity, of a large number of Canadian industries. In other words, it would generally take several Canadian industries to equal just one of these giant United States corporations. Each one of these big United States corporations carries on extensive research work within their own ambit. Research, as is well known, leads to economies of production; it leads to benefits to the public; it leads to benefits to the workingman; it leads to benefits generally to the national economy.
One of our problems is that researchwise we are very deficient as compared with the United States. In the field of industry it is
4346	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act surely self-evident that very few of our individual industries can begin to compete re-searchwise with these giant United States corporations. It, therefore, seems to me to be equally self-evident that it is desirable if we can bring about a situation in Canada under which our industries can pool their facilities for research, so that together, co-operatively, they can begin to compete in this one field alone with what is carried on in the United States by their competitors.
We were faced, therefore, with the problem of whether we could find a legislative device or a legislative provision which would permit the carrying on of a co-operative arrangement between industries in Canada to produce this desirable objective without, at the same time, providing a cloak or umbrella, if you like, under which industries could in fact combine in a manner contrary to the best interests of the economy and of the public generally. We came to the conclusion that we could devise such a legislative formula, and we came to the further conclusion it would be in the interests of the Canadian economy for us to do so. This is the reason for this provision in the amending bill before the house. I am prepared to defend that provision in debate here and in debate elsewhere.
I was dealing, before I went into this aside, although it is an important aside, with the amendments conducive to the second of the two main objectives I have mentioned, that is the objective of bringing the law up to date and making it fit with the twentieth century economy. I should like to conclude this list of such provisions by mentioning the amendments establishing new methods of procedure. I should like to emphasize here that these amendments are contemplated by and, indeed, recommended by the MacQuarrie committee report.
I would suggest without hesitation that all the amendments before the house are faithful to the history and spirit of anti-combines legislation as it has existed over the years, but they have the advantage that they bring this legislation up to date; they bring it into line with the needs of the mid-twentieth century economy. They not only accomplish this objective, but they do so while obtaining a workable and effective system of legislation against antisocial combines or arrangements. They do so also while at the same time bringing a degree of protection to the small businessman who is so vital to our continued free economy.
It is against this background I should like now to give a more detailed discussion of the actual provisions of the amending bill. I will begin by discussing the substantive changes, then the changes of a procedural


nature and I should like to conclude by a few remarks on the amendments of a consequential nature. I am aware, Mr. Speaker, of the rule against discussion of the details of a bill, and particularly of the clauses, in a debate on second reading. I shall do all I can not to transgress the prohibitions of the rule. It is, however, difficult, as I know you will appreciate and as my colleagues in the house will appreciate, to discuss an amending bill which contains a lot of particular amendments without some discussion of the reasons for the amendments. Therefore, while I will attempt to avoid reference to the clauses in detail, I should like to assist the house by discussing the arguments, if you like, which have given rise to these specific amendments.
First, in so far as the substantive changes are concerned, it will have been noted, I am sure, that the provisions of the Criminal Code relating to combinations in restraint of trade are moved out of the Criminal Code and into the Combines Investigation Act. The result will be, when the new bill passes, that the Combines Investigation Act will contain all the anti-combines legislation. Sections 411, 412 and 416 of the Criminal Code would then be repealed. There are a variety of arguments, which have been made both for and against this proposition. Many of them were summarized in the MacQuarrie committee report to which I have referred. After listening to the representations and discussing them in detail with those who made them, as well as reviewing the MacQuarrie committee study, we came to the conclusion that in view of the desirability of achieving certainty and clarification in the combines legislation, and in view of the changing nature of economic conditions, it would be desirable to consolidate all the provisions into the one combines act.
But I should point out here that the definition of a combine as contained in the Criminal Code has been retained. All that has been done in effect is to transfer it from the Criminal Code into the Combines Investigation Act. It is this definition which was the operative definition under which the great majority of cases were brought and under which definitive jurisprudence has been developed. This definition is contained, with only consequential changes in the wording, in the new bill.
Other substantive amendments deal with the desirability of ensuring that the combines law does not become so rigid that, while discouraging the doing of that which is antisocial and which has been in effect defined by the jurisprudence as being subject to condemnation by the courts, it might also

deprive society and the country of the benefit of practices or developments that are not only not harmful but indeed are positively beneficial. Thus, while combines in restraint of trade, combines which fix prices or discourage competition or prevent entry into trade or industry-all those combines which over the years legislation and the courts have declared to be harmful and have prohibited subject to heavy penalty-while these are still left under the full condemnation and operation of the undiluted law, nevertheless it is recognized in the legislation that certain forms of co-operation are beneficial.
A few moments ago I mentioned one of the forms of co-operation, namely that in research, which will itself be beneficial to the economy generally. Other forms of co-operation which it is recognized may be beneficial are enumerated in the bill, particularly in clause 32. Perhaps I should not mention the clause in detail, but one of them that I might mention generally is the exchange of credit information. There are six of them that are specifically mentioned, all of which we believe can be demonstrated to be positively beneficial to society and to the economy generally.
To give effect to this principle the bill first repeats the definition of a combine as contained in the Criminal Code. Incidentally, I should point out that the word "unduly", of which mention has been made in certain newspaper articles, was always there. It has been there since a Conservative government first enacted it in 1889 and it is still there. The bill repeats the combines definition of the code, but then in order to carry out this principle I have enunciated it provides that there shall be no conviction if the cooperative arrangement relates to only one or more of the demonstrably beneficial purposes, two of which I have mentioned. The others are spelled out in the bill.
Finally, in order to make assurance doubly sure that there can be no possibility of carrying on an illegitimate type of combine activity, the bill concludes in this respect by making it clear that the defence of beneficial arrangement cannot be used as a cloak or umbrella under which to carry on an antisocial or illegitimate type of combine activity.
If I add that all of the combination cases that have been dealt with by the courts under the anti-combine legislation have been cases of price fixing it will be seen that the present bill does not affect the law against price fixing and any combination case of any kind under which a conviction was secured in Canada would be equally liable to secure a conviction under the amended provision; but at the same time we hope this amendment will contribute to alleviate the concern of
Combines Investigation Act legitimate business and make it clear that they may engage in activities which would benefit the Canadian economy and that if they confine their co-operative activities to these beneficial activities they need have no fear of prosecution or conviction under the combines legislation.
I should like next to draw the attention of the house to a second group of amendments affecting the substance of the Combines Investigation Act. It relates to a certain number of trade practices and aims toward a legitimate degree of protection for smaller business against what would otherwise be the unrestricted and dominating economic strength of their more powerful competitors. In this second group there are four amendments of particular importance. One relates to the practice of loss leader selling and other similar practices. Another relates to making more efficient the present provisions of the Criminal Code which are translated into the Combines Investigation Act, regarding discriminatory pricing. Another deals with promotional allowances and finally there is an amendment affecting misleading advertising.
With relation to the amendment affecting loss leader selling and related practices, it will be recalled that when section 34 of the Combines Investigation Act was passed in 1951 we as the opposition took the stand that it was being passed in undue haste and without consideration of the safeguards that would be necessary to protect smaller merchants against the practice of loss leader selling which we believe this section would encourage. We have received in detail a large number of complaints from small merchants and their organizations with regard to the practice of loss leader prices and certain other undesirable practices that have become prevalent with the results that we feared.
May I emphasize that in virtually every case the representations received in this field came from small business or their representatives, not from large concerns or from the manufacturers. The representations we received were to the effect that small business is powerless to protect itself and that small businessmen are powerless to protect themselves against the power of a large concern; that their interest in continuing as an established outlet of a known line of goods is jeopardized and therefore their ability to continue in business at all is at stake. Anyone who is familiar in any way with the interests and the operations of small business I think will appreciate the urgency of these representations.
We are satisfied that the practices of which they complain and which they brought to our attention are not in general beneficial to

Combines Investigation Act consumers. Many of the practices complained of are based on one form or another of misrepresentation with regard to the availability of the goods or with regard to the standard of services to be provided by the person or concern that sells them or by some other come-on device which the consumer finds, to his disadvantage, has misled him when he purchased the goods. Some of these practices constitute an attack on the legitimate interests of both the established retailer and the manufacturer in regard to the reputation, the quality and the availability of the goods and all of them operate to the detriment both of the retailer and in the long run of the consumer himself.
There are therefore in this field two problems. The first is how to get at this situation and find an effective method of dealing with it without doing the consumer or the retailer a disservice or eliminating the genuine type of sale and therefore eliminating the possibility of reduced price advantage.
The second problem is how to do this without getting into the field of such detailed regulation of trade and business as to be impracticable and undesirable, if not actually unconstitutional, for the federal government to embark upon.
Notwithstanding these problems we were determined, for the reasons I have given, to protect the legitimate interests and position of the small businessman whom we still regard as the backbone of a truly free economy. We regard it as desirable to retain the maximum number of independent operators. We regard it as desirable to ensure that we shall not end up with the position where everyone is working for someone else, whether it be a giant corporation or the government.
The problem is difficult, and there have been criticisms, I know, of the solutions we have found. It would have been easy enough to have taken the attitude: let her rip, after all it is a free economy; let it find its own level. The giant corporations would have been happy, but I do not think we would have been doing a proper service or doing our duty to the Canadian public generally. So we determined to find a solution, and I believe the solution we have found meets both the problems that I mentioned a few moments ago.
The solution in general provides that if supplies to merchants are discontinued only for one of the legitimate reasons mentioned in the legislation and not for the illegitimate purpose of forcing a manufacturer's price level on the public, then there is no offence. Such an answer would be a defence to a prosecution, if one should be brought. This


amendment to section 34 has two beneficial results. First, it is in clarification of the law. I want to make this clear: it does not restore resale price maintenance, in spite of what the Winnipeg Free Press said, but it will bring about a situation where small businessmen may be helped to meet practices which confer no lasting benefit on the consumer and which are as undesirable from a consumer standpoint as from that of competitors and manufacturers. It should help the small merchant to stay in business so long as he is efficient, to the advantage of the consumer and of the economy generally without the danger of his being callously eliminated by the mere power of a rival's purse. It will also tend to prevent the monopolization of certain trades by particular merchants through the instrumentality of unfair and undesirable business practices. At the same time the amendment does not prevent downward pressure upon prices which are occasioned by the ability of some merchants, due to their efficiency or methods of operation, to sell at prices lower than others, nor does it restrain the genuine clearance sale.
Another amendment to which I should like to draw the attention of the house is the one relating to what is presently section 412 of the Criminal Code, which will become section 33A of the Combines Investigation Act. This section, in part, forbids businessmen to follow a policy of selling articles in any part of Canada at lower prices than they charge elsewhere in Canada, where that policy has or is designed to have the effect of substantially lessening competition or eliminating a competitor, and it also forbids the policy of selling articles anywhere at prices unreasonably low, having or designed to have the same effect. In operation it was found that the requirement which the crown had to meet was such as to make this section of little effect. It has therefore been amended to provide that if the policy has a tendency to substantially lessen competition or eliminate a competitor, this is sufficient to constitute the offence.
A third amendment in this group would insert a new provision dealing with promotional allowances. A report of the restrictive trade practices commission published in 1958 and relating to discriminatory pricing in the grocery trade pointed out that a common source of discrimination lay in promotional allowances lying outside the scope of present legislation. It has been decided to eliminate the element of discrimination to which this report pointed, and the new section therefore provides that where a merchant or other supplier grants promotional allowances, he must do so on a reasonably proportionate basis to all his competing customers. I might

also add in this connection that the recent report of the royal commission on price spreads of food products stressed the desirability of restricting promotional allowances in favour of price reductions as a method of competition. While it might, on first view, appear paradoxical to try to achieve this purpose by requiring that promotional allowances, where granted, be without discrimination, we believe that this provision is likely to have the effect of discouraging such promotional allowances by the very fact of requiring that if granted at all they be granted generally to competing customers. And certainly if it does not have this result it will at least restore equality of competition as between large and small merchants by requiring such an allowance to be granted proportionately to all purchasers.
The fourth and last amendment to which I wish to refer in this group is a new section forbidding anyone, for the purpose of promoting the sale or use of an article, to make a materially misleading representation to the public concerning the price at which such article is ordinarily sold. Quite a few instances have come to the attention of the combines branch, some of them occurring in the catalogues of so-called catalogue houses, but occurring in other places as well, where a merchant, in order to make it appear that the price at which he was offering an article was more favourable than was actually the case, misrepresented to the public the price at which such article was ordinarily sold elsewhere. Besides being deceptive as far as the buying public is concerned this practice also constitutes an unfair method of competition with respect to other merchants.
In summary, these amendments relating to discriminatory and predatory pricing and deceptive price advertising have a multiple purpose and effect. In all instances they directly or indirectly protect the consumer and will bring greater honesty into all branches of trade. In some instances they also protect, or give a chance for protection, to merchants, usually the smaller merchants, against unfair competition which does not relate to competitive efficiency; they confirm to a manufacturer some right to prevent his product from being abused or used as a come-on device; and, finally, but not least, they are in the long term direction of maintaining competition by cutting down practices or assisting in the prevention of practices which may serve to eliminate competitors and therefore competition through means other than straightforward and real competition itself.
May I now draw the attention of the house to certain amendment of a procedural nature. I should mention a procedural innovation of
Combines Investigation Act particular interest. It consists of conferring upon the Exchequer Court of Canada concurrent jurisdiction with that of the superior courts of the provinces to try the more serious of the anti-combines offences or to entertain applications for orders of injunction or dissolution. This jurisdiction of the exchequer court could only be invoked, in the case of a prosecution, with the consent of the accused and of the crown, and the section is made subject to proclamation by the governor in council in order to permit us to consider what arrangements might be necessary for its implementation. Such a procedure, we believe, would be very beneficial to all parties concerned, since it would lead to more expeditious and less expensive handling of cases; it would also eventually develop a corps of judges expert in anti-combines jurisprudence and permit such cases to be presented to the court by members of the bar of any province. This seems only fair in view of the fact that major anticombines cases ordinarily extend over a number or even all of the provinces and have effects beyond the province in which the venue for trial is ordinarily laid. May I again emphasize in this connection that the procedure of reference to the exchequer court in the case of a prosecution for a completed offence or an action in respect to a completed offence can only be followed at the instance of the crown with the consent of the accused.
In addition, by way of other procedural amendments, the bill would permit as an alternative to prosecution leading to conviction and fine or imprisonment an action directed to obtain an injunction or, in the case of a merger an order of dissolution, even in a case where the offence has already been completed. Such an action may already be brought in the case of an incipient offence but the wording of the section leaves in doubt, at least, whether it could be invoked where the offence has been completed.
In the case, for example, of price fixing combinations the law is now clearly established and it is not intended to apply the amendment in such cases. Everybody knows what a combine is and prosecution and conviction are the appropriate procedures there, but there are other cases where the difference between legality and illegality may depend upon a pretty fine judgment on the part of the parties concerned and their counsel. It seems appropriate that in such cases it should be possible to redress the situation by other means.
May I emphasize here, too, that this is an alternative procedure the choice of which will lie with the prosecuting authority and that it will provide a speedier method of disposing of appropriate cases and of building

Combines Investigation Act up a body of jurisprudence, while still leaving it open to prosecute in the ordinary way where the appropriate course is prosecution and conviction. Because a great deal has been made of this in places outside this house, may I again emphasize here that this also is inherent in the recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee which reported in 1952.
Next comes an amendment which will be a useful guide to the department. May I pause here for a moment to say that one of the difficulties of the present law is that it is a difficult one to interpret and apply. We do not want to relieve ourselves of this difficulty simply for our own convenience but we think it would be desirable to resolve or remove the difficulty if possible in order that the application of the act and the remedies under the act might be more clear, more certain and more speedy because this is certainly in the best interests of the government as well as the parties concerned and the economy generally.
There will be a useful guide to the department in the new amendment, in determining whether the appropriate remedy lies in a prosecution or in a suit for an injunction to restrain the further operation of the combination. It would also make clearer to the public the nature of the combination which was made the subject of an investigation and a report. This amendment in question adds to the terms of reference of the restrictive trade practices commission by directing the commission in the case of a combination to make a specific finding as to whether or not the combination relates to practices such as price fixing, which parliament and the courts have unequivocally condemned, or other like practices; or whether it relates to one or more of the other matters which I have described as matters in respect of which cooperation among firms is not necessarily to the public detriment. The amendment also requires the commission, if it finds that the combination relates to one of these latter matters, to make a further finding whether, in spite of the appearance of the combination, it does adversely affect competition in respect of prices, entry to market or like matters.
The last group of provisions in this bill are what I have called consequential amendments of a mainly ancillary nature. Certain definitions have been inserted for convenient reference. Certain sections have undergone clarification or other changes necessarily incidental to the main provisions which I have mentioned. Here I should merely like to draw the attention of the house to an amendment in relation to mergers. The section making it an offence to be party to a merger

remains in effect the same. However, hon. members will notice that a new definition of the merger has been introduced in the Combines Investigation Act.
In the present legislation we have a composite expression "merger, trust or monopoly", which is given an all-embracing definition. It has been found that the word "trust" is really redundant and that the first part of the definition may be said to relate to a merger and the second part to a monopoly. It was decided, therefore, to remove the word "trust" and with this and the removal of the definition of "combination" to a new section which, as explained, carries forward the present Criminal Code definition, a rewording of the present definition section became necessary. There is no change in the effect of the definition of merger but it is made clear that the gist of the offence is the lessening or the likelihood of lessening competition and that the degree of lessening which is necessary in order to constitute the offence is a degree that the court would find to be against the interest of the public. At the same time, it was decided to give the court a measure of guidance by indicating that it might look for a lessening of competition, in the case of mergers, not only in horizontal integration but also in vertical integration.
I have tried Mr. Speaker, to give the house a fairly comprehensive description of the significant provisions of the bill. I shall expect to add some details later on as the house proceeds with its study of the legislation. But before concluding I should, I think, say a word or two about some of the changes in the present bill as compared to the bill introduced into the house last year. Here I wish to refer primarily to modifications with respect to combinations and mergers. Representations were received concerning the drafting of clause 32 in last year's bill. Businessmen and lawyers in particular feared that our amendment actually resulted in a shifting of the burden of proof from the crown to the accused. Let me say first that such a thing was never in the contemplation or intention of the government and we think the fears expressed were misplaced and exaggerated, but there were fears and they were expressed forcibly and genuinely. In order to make the situation clear, therefore, we have redrafted section 32 so that there can be no doubt whatever that the burden of proof lies upon the crown as has always been the case in the anti-combines legislation.
Second, certain provisions with regard to mergers have been dropped After reconsidering all of the factors involved and in view of the fact that a number of cases relating to mergers are now before the courts or before the restrictive trade practices commission we

decided that it would be preferable not to proceed with any change in the substantive law with regard to the merger provisions for the time being. When a larger body of jurisprudence has been developed as a result of the cases before the courts or before the commission and when several reports of the commission have been made public then we will be in a position to give consideration to whatever amendments may be required in this connection.
In the latter part of my remarks I have been discussing the bill itself and some of the changes in this bill as compared with last year's bill. I have endeavoured to be as noncontroversial as appropriate or possible in a discussion of legislation of this kind and particularly with regard to the presentation of the material in the bill itself I have tried to make a factual presentation. I hope to conclude my remarks in that same vein. I do not think, however, that I can overlook in this connection some remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in the course of the annual meeting of the association of his party. He said at that time, in effect, that our enforcement of the Combines Investigation Act was not such as his party would engage in; they believed in anticombines legislation but they would not, in contrast to us, persecute big business.
I think I should point out that what we have been doing since we assumed office is enforcing as fairly, impartially and vigorously as possible legislation with respect to which all the most recent parts were placed on the statute books by the Liberal government. I think, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that in fairness I may challenge the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) that before this debate is concluded he must either justify his innuendo of our persecution of business or stand branded as one who makes remarks of this sort for the sake of political advantage.
Something you have never been known to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would be interested to hear what the Leader of the Opposition has to say in this respect; but perhaps it is also fair to note that the attitude of the official opposition at any rate has been revealed for us in part by some other remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition in a television broadcast in January of this year. I suppose to some extent we might have been left in the dark otherwise if the hon. gentleman had not thus revealed his hand, although we probably would not have been quite so much in the dark as to the attitude of the C.C.F. group in this house. But I recall that in January of this year the Leader of the
Combines Investigation Act Opposition told the country in the course of a television broadcast that the Liberals in parliament would strongly oppose the government's forthcoming amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. This, mind you, Mr. Speaker, was said before the details of our present amendments had ever been revealed.
Mr. Pearson. The bill had been distributed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not the new bill. It is a difficult task to enlighten or to undertake to enlighten persons who have indicated such a preconceived and prejudiced view of legislation which is going to be introduced.
It was introduced last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have said that the details of the present amendments were not known to the house or to the hon. gentleman when he made that statement, and I stand by what I say. It is difficult to suppose that we shall be able to enlighten those persons who take such a preconceived and prejudiced view in advance of the bill, but we shall do our best. We are prepared to defend the legislation and to discuss it, and to discuss any points which my hon. friends may bring forward.
We remember also another occasion-I do not think it is inapt to recall it here-in this parliament. In 1956 statements were made outside the house with regard to the attitude to be taken by the opposition with respect to legislation to be introduced by the government of that day. I remember that we said we were going to oppose the legislation vigorously and violently and to the utmost of our ability. I also remember closure-I also remember, Mr. Speaker, that that indication of our attitude on that occasion called forth the immediate application of closure by the government so that the House of Commons might not have the opportunity which the opposition wished to have of discussing the legislation freely and fully.
Mr. Speaker, times have changed. I regret the preconceived and prejudiced attitude of the opposition revealed in that television statement, but I assure the Leader of the Opposition, and all hon. members opposite, that they will have the fullest and freest opportunity to discuss this legislation because we believe in it. We believe it to be sound. We know it to be for the advantage of the people of Canada and we shall be interested indeed to listen to and to have the opportunity of meeting and of refuting the points and arguments to be advanced against it. I can only say that if the arguments advanced against it are the same as those advanced in

Combines Investigation Act some of the press of this country supporting my hon. friend's party they will not be very difficult to refute.
Now if I may be permitted a short departure from the spirit of non-controversial discussion and coming back to the bill itself, I can assure the house that a great deal of study has gone into the provisions which we have introduced. We believe that they represent a substantial improvement over the law as it exists at the present time, but we recognize that neither the members of the government-certainly I speak for myself anyway; perhaps I should not speak for my colleagues in this way-nor the members of any department are the sole repositories of all wisdom or all knowledge and' ideas in the field of anti-combines legislation. We recognize also that there is a very great deal of interest and naturally a very real concern on the part of practically every segment of our community, of our society and of our economy in connection with provisions of this nature, and that there is a very real and understandable desire to make representations about them publicly and to have the opportunity of discussing them in public with members of this house.
It is, therefore, our intention, as soon as the house may have given second reading to the bill to refer it to a committee-we think the appropriate committee would be the committee on banking and commerce-for study by that committee in order that members of parliament may have an opportunity, in the atmosphere which committee study makes possible, to consider the provisions of the bill and in order that individuals and organizations may have the opportunity to make representations and to discuss it there with the members of this house who will be called upon eventually to enact the provisions. We are prepared, in other words, to submit the details of our proposals to the detailed discussion and detailed judgment of parliament itself.
While we believe that our proposals, within the framework of the present principles, are as adequate and as far-reaching as at the moment we should submit to the house, nevertheless I can assure the house that our attitude is not rigid. If, after listening to the representations that may be made before the committee and discussing those representations with those who may appear there, the committee feels that improvements in detail can be made they will find the government by no means inflexible in its attitude toward the suggestions, the desires and the expressions of opinion of the committee.
