But subject only, as I say, to this readiness to submit it to a committee and to maintain a flexible and reasonable attitude with regard


to suggestions for improvement which may be made, I conclude by saying that our amendments to the Combines Investigation Act will increase the flexibility, the efficiency and the enforceability of anti-combines legislation in Canada. We believe that they bring the law up to date in a realistic manner and make it possible for industry to operate in ways which will be beneficial to the public while at the same time restraining those operations which are harmful to the public interest, that they provide protection to the legitimate interests of small business and in every way produce, within the limitations of the present principles, a beneficial and far-reaching improvement in the legislation in the general interests of this nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house will have listened with great interest to the minister's statement about the amendments to this legislation. The minister will not be surprised when I tell him that we on this side have listened with more interest than agreement.
I participate in this debate, Mr. Speaker, branded by the minister. His brand, as it applies to me, means that my remarks will have to take a little longer than they otherwise would because it will take a little time, although it will not require much effort, to remove the particular brand which he saw fit to apply to me in closing the remarks of what he said was a very non-controversial and non-political speech.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, in the circumstances it may be necessary later on to discuss some of his own statements beginning in September, 1958 and continuing through 1959 in support of legislation which he introduced into this house and then was forced to withdraw because it was premature and ill conceived. In the face of that record, Mr. Speaker, in the face of that legislation, in the face of the minister's statements about that legislation, to complain that we on this side said we would oppose such legislation if it were introduced again and that we would oppose the attitude of the government toward this legislation as already proposed, shows that the minister is a very sensitive person indeed.
The bill before us, as the minister pointed out, does not introduce new legislation. It is an amendment to existing legislation rather than a revision, as he pointed out, of the legislation which is now in effect. But it is a very important and very far-reaching amendment of most important legislation. While we on this side have no desire to prolong the debate unduly because, as the minister indicated, the bill if it gets second reading will go to a committee, nevertheless

in view of the importance of the legislation and the importance of the amendments in the bill they will have to be examined with all the care which that importance warrants.
I am going to begin, Mr. Speaker, at what normally would be the end of my speech and put on the record at once a summary of the position that we will adopt in respect of these amendments and a summary of the position of the Liberal party with respect to monopolistic situations and restrictive trade practices which are covered by the amendments. Having summarized our position in this way, I will then proceed to try to substantiate in detail some of the objections to the legislation which will be mentioned in the summary.
We on this side believe that in the circumstances Canada faces today and has faced now for a good many years, a mixed economic system is the most appropriate form of economic organization for the development of our country; a mixed economic system composed of a public sector, a co-operative sector and a private enterprise sector. We also believe that the private enterprise sector should be as large but only as large as compatible with the public interest and that it should be governed by the competitive rule applied in free markets, having regard, however, as the minister mentioned during his speech, to the changing nature of economic circumstances and the changing nature of economic development.
In that sense we believe that the present Combines Investigation Act with certain administrative amendments-I am going to mention one or two which I think should be made-is adequate to achieve these objectives, particularly the last objective I have mentioned.
Under our present set-up-these are some of the changes which I think might be made in the principle of this legislation-the director of investigation and research has wide powers of investigation. This is as it should be although I say now, as I have said before outside the house, that all possible abuses of those powers should be avoided in order to ensure justice and fairness for all, including businesses, and so that the public respect for this legislation and its procedures will be strong. Moreover, concrete and empirical research on monopolistic situations and practices should in our view be greatly expanded and a special research division should be created under the authority of the director in the present legislation.
Finally, we think that the hearing before the restrictive trade practices commission and the report it publishes in each case should not be a mere preliminary step to a criminal prosecution. As the present act says, that report should "appraise the effect on the public
Combines Investigation Act interest of arrangements and practices disclosed in the evidence" and should contain recommendations in each case as to remedies other than criminal prosecution and specifically designed to correct a given undesirable situation.
Those three suggestions would in our view represent major improvements in the present legislation and would make Canadian combines policy more flexible and more effective. The minister had a good deal to say about flexibility. To be implemented these changes would not require any change in the present act at all.
While we suggest that some administrative changes can be made to make the present legislation more effective, we are strongly opposed to the bill now before us to amend the Combines Investigation Act. We believe, notwithstanding what the minister has said, that the bill will weaken the act, that it will facilitate undesirable private control over the economy and, in particular, that it will injure the interests of the consumers. I may be wrong but I do not recall the minister mentioning the consumers in his hour and a half speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You did not listen very carefully then.
If he did I accept his word. He did not dwell very much on the interests of the consumers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Again you did not listen very carefully.

We will read the minister's speech tomorrow and we will see who was right. We have several minor objections to the bill which will be presented at a later stage of the discussion, but our main objection, and at the moment the only one I will deal with, is on three fundamental points of principle.
As the minister pointed out in some detail, the bill permits firms within an industry to pursue certain joint activities provided those joint activities, those combinations if you like, do not have the effect of lessening competition unduly in respect of prices, production, markets, distribution or the number of units within an industry. In order to decide whether or not those joint activities, those combined activities, are objectionable the courts will have to appraise their effects. There is no other way of doing it.
The courts have not been asked in the past to make such an appraisal and the courts themselves have contended that they were not equipped to make it. So, and surely this is an important point, the courts may well be put in a position where they will have to interpret this new provision in such a way as

Combines Investigation Act to exempt, for all practical purposes, a great variety of joint activities from the operation of the act. I will come back to this in more detail later. If that is the case, parliament might as well exempt all combinations from the act. That is why we believe this particular new provision, whatever may have been its intention, does indeed have very dangerous implications.
Up to now when an offence has been committed under the act the only recognized procedure was criminal prosecution. If the accused were found guilty they were liable to a heavy fine or to imprisonment. This bill, as the minister pointed out, now provides for an alternative procedure whereby the minister on his own discretion can simply inform the courts that an offence has been committed and merely ask the courts to issue an order prohibiting the continuation of the offence. We on this side have grave doubts as to the constitutionality of that particular provision because it contemplates a civil remedy for what is a criminal offence. Moreover, it gives rise to the possibility of undesirable discrimination. For the same offence, and at the discretion of the minister, different persons will be liable to a heavy fine and imprisonment or subject merely to a court order prohibiting the continuation of the offence. Finally, this relatively mild procedure will remove the preventive value of present remedies and will create a great inducement, in our view, to form combinations and monopolies.
The practice of resale price maintenance will continue to be prohibited in theory. Perhaps in view of the attitude of the minister and some of his colleagues with regard to resale price maintenance in 1956 we have a right to be a little surprised that they left it in the act, but they have in theory. They have in this bill, notwithstanding what the minister said tonight, ensured that resale price maintenance can be reintroduced through the back door by a technique which will amount to a system of private law. As I shall try to point out in detail later, it imposes a kind of commercial feudalism. A manufacturer or supplier will be in a position to enforce at his own discretion, if this bill becomes law, a series of vague and arbitrary provisions affecting the retailer. He will be entitled to refuse to sell his products to a dealer on the basis of reports made to him by informers who will often, in the normal course of things, be competitors of that particular dealer.
Under such a system, therefore, the manufacturer cannot be an impartial, free judge. He will be exposed to constant pressures


from retailers wishing to eliminate competitors and to prevent price cutting. Under the new provisions, if they become law, the manufacturer will be caught between the courts, if he tries to enforce a scheme of resale price maintenance, and retailers urging him to enforce such a scheme. He may certainly find it more difficult to carry on his own business under such conditions.
In so far as the retailer is concerned, he will not be free under this bill, if it becomes law, to conduct his own business as he wishes. He will always be liable to denunciation by a competitor and to arbitrary arrangements by a manufacturer. The grounds giving rise to such a denunciation and arrangements are numerous. They are vague, and they may well hurt the independent small retailer far more than the big chain stores. In any case, these new provisions will create a very unhealthy climate in the whole sector of the retail trade.
Finally, and most important, if these new provisions are implemented the main victim will be the man who so often has nobody to speak for him, the consumer. His choice will be restricted and the prices he will have to pay will be higher. The only way, under this provision, that the manufacturer can live in peace with retailers will be to determine a higher resale price for his products and include a reasonable mark-up. The only way that the retailer can live in peace with his competitors, and avoid getting into trouble, will be to maintain the resale prices determined by the manufacturer. If peace is maintained, therefore, among manufacturers and retailers it will only be at the expense of the consumer who will be the forgotten person in so far as this new deal is concerned.
If the government feels that some of the practices it is asking the manufacturer to prevent, asking the supplier to prevent, are really undesirable from the point of view of the public interest, then surely the only fair and honourable course of action to take is to make those practices illegal and let the courts decide when an offence has been committed. A system of private law, even if it is to be governed under the supervision of the courts, is not acceptable. What about the civil rights of the individual with respect to this particular provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are not affected under this law.
The minister will have a hard time convincing us of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is obvious; you made up your mind before you even saw it.

The Conservative party in 1919, and during the regime of the Right Hon.

R. B. Bennett, attempted to weaken our combines legislation, as I will point out later in detail. I shall try to correct some of the historical distortions of my hon. friend the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You do not like history lessons, do you?

It will be easy to do that, and I propose to do it. The Conservative party is now trying to do the same thing again in respect of this law in a different way. Well, we on this side will fight as vigorously as possible to prevent this third attempt from succeeding because there have been two preceding ones. In so doing we will hope to safeguard competition as the governing rule of the free enterprise sector of the economy, to protect the necessary freedom of enterprise within our mixed economy and in the interest of the consumer. This bill does none of those things.
That, Mr. Speaker, is our position in principle in regard to this particular bill. It does, as the minister has said and as I have said myself a few moments ago, introduce some important amendments to one of our most important pieces of legislation in this country, the combines legislation, which has been in existence since 1910.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Since 1889.
We will come back to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Remaking history.

The first combines act was passed in 1910. That legislation imposed upon an important sector of our economy, namely the industrial sector-the importance of which the minister has stressed and which is, of course, obvious to us all-a specific structure and definite standards of behaviour. This bill, if it is passed, will change that structure and will weaken those standards. That is why, having stated our position on the general principle, it is important also to understand the history leading up to this legislation and the basic and historical differences between the two parties on this subject of combines legislation.
The minister talked about combines legislation going back to 1889 introduced by a Conservative government. It is certainly true that the provision in the Criminal Code dealing with combines was introduced by a Conservative government in 1889. It is also perfectly true that the Conservative party, in the years during which it was in office after that time, did nothing to make this provision of the Criminal Code effective. The minister knows that the enforcement of the Criminal Code is the responsibility of the
Combines Investigation Act provinces. There was no administrative machinery. There was no Combines Investigation Act setting up any machinery to make this provision effective.
The minister may also perhaps know

and his experts will tell him if he does not know -that the first prosecution under this piece of Conservative criminal legislation was in 1903 when a Liberal government was in power. During the years 1889 to 1903 there was not a single prosecution under a Conservative administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Business was honest under a Conservative government.

The minister perhaps also
knows, because he is a student of history, about the experience of Canada from 1900 to 1910 in respect to mergers and the development of monopolies. He perhaps also knows that in 1910 a Liberal government took notice of this situation and passed-Right Hon. Mackenzie King was the minister who introduced the legislation-the first Combines Investigation Act in our history to make this provision of the Criminal Code effective. The minister may also know-if he does not know, he might look it up-that action was taken after 1910 under that act until 1919 when the Conservative party was in power again. They then destroyed the Combines Investigation Act or introduced legislation of their own which had that effect but which was later declared unconstitutional.
In the course of time-and it was not very long because there is never a very long gap in these matters-in 1923 the Liberals were in power again and a new Combines Investigation Act was passed by a Liberal government, the earlier one having been destroyed by a Conservative government. That act of 1923 is essentially the legislation we have on the statute books today. That law, in contrast to the Conservative law from 1889 to 1903 in the Criminal Code-I refer to the law of 1923-was effectively enforced until 1930. There were several investigations and prosecutions under that law and a vigorous anti-monopoly policy was enforced by the government of that particular day.
Then we came to 1930 when we had another Conservative government which in effect suspended once more the operation of that act. In 1935, as a result of a royal commission of which I have some memory because I was the secretary of that particular royal commission, the Conservative government of Mr. Bennett introduced the Dominion Trade and Industry Act which provided for the acceptance of almost any kind of combine, monopoly and restrictive trade

Combines Investigation Act practice if the commission set up by this act so recommended on the ground that it would prevent wasteful competition, would not unduly restrain trade or operate against public interest. The recommendations of this commission were to be approved by the governor in council and it thus brought the operations of this commission under the authority of the government. Therefore under this act, instead of competition, the government through order in council would be in a position to regulate the activities of the private sector of our economy. Not only did this change have dangerous implications for the economy and not only was it prejudicial 1 believe to the public interest, but it was also found by the courts to be unconstitutional.
So in 1936, with a Liberal government again in power, we had to start all over again and restore the act of 1923 with some improvements. What happened then? This history, Mr. Speaker, is very interesting, especially in the light of the version we were given by the minister. What happened to this legislation of 1936? In contrast to the situation we have in parliament today, and though this legislation was passed by the House of Commons it was thrown out by a Tory majority in the Senate. Mr. King, then prime minister, introduced it again in 1937 and it was allowed to go through. On the second occasion time it was allowed to go

through a Conservative Senate. In 1946 the act was modified, as we know. In 1951 some important administrative changes were made and there was the prohibition of resale price maintenance against which my hon. friends opposite fought day in and day out and which they swore they would remove from the statute books if they ever had the chance to do so. However, it is still there in spite of these amendments.
In 1952 there was a further amendment which changed the administrative set-up of the act and I believe established the restrictive trade practices commission. That is the history behind this legislation. That is the position taken by the Conservative party over the years with regard to combines legislation. In the face of that record the minister has told us this evening that his party from 1889 had always stood behind the combines legislation and against monopolies and mergers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Quite right. We introduced it.
